And with us today is our case manager, Ms. Lourdes Galicia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to explain how we are going to proceed during this hearing. As the registrar announced, the case on our agenda is Prosecutor versus Radislav Krstic. This is an appeal against the judgement issued by the Trial Chamber on the 2nd of August, 2001. The Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Krstic of genocide under Article 4 of the Tribunal's Statute for his alleged role in the execution of between 7.000 and 8.000 Bosnian Muslim men following the fall of Srebrenica. This was Count 1 of the indictment. Mr. Krstic was also convicted of persecution as a crime against humanity under Article 4 -- 5 -- under Article 5 for acts committed between 10th and 13th of July, 1995. This was a part of Count 6 of the indictment. Finally, Mr. Krstic was convicted of murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war under Article 3 of the Tribunal's Statute. This conviction was for Count 5 of the indictment. The Trial Chamber acquitted Mr. Krstic of complicity to commit genocide, this was Count 2; and of deportation as a crime against humanity, this was Count 7. The Trial Chamber also did not enter a number of convictions on the ground that they would be impermissibly cumulative. These were convictions for extermination as a crime against humanity, Count 3; murder as a crime against humanity under Article 5, Count 4; persecution under Article 5, with respect to acts committed between 13th and 19th of July, 1995 - this was a part of Count 6 - and inhumane acts or, alternatively, forcible transfer as a crime against humanity under Article 5, Count 8. Mr. Krstic was sentenced to a single sentence of imprisonment for 46 years. Both Mr. Krstic and the Prosecution appealed the judgement. This past Friday we have heard arguments concerning the weight and credibility of the additional evidence and of rebuttal material admitted in this appeal. Today and tomorrow we will hear arguments on the merits of the appeal. Today we are proceeding in the absence of Judge Schomburg pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Rule 15 bis (A) permits a hearing to continue in the absence of a Judge where, for illness or other urgent personal reasons or for reasons of authorised Tribunal business, he's unable to continue sitting in a part-heard case for a period which is likely to be of short duration and the remaining Judges of the Chamber are satisfied that it is in the interest of justice to do so. Justice Schomburg is away on Tribunal authorised business and he will join us again tomorrow. His absence has been discussed by the remaining Judges, and we are satisfied that it is in the interest of justice that we proceed with today's hearings. Before giving the floor to counsel for both parties, I will summarise the grounds of appeal presented by the parties in their written submissions. The first ground of appeal of the Prosecution concerns cumulative convictions. The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in vacating as cumulative convictions in relations to Count 3, which is extermination; Count 6, persecution as a crime against humanity for the murders committed between 13th and 19th of July, 1995; Count 4, murder as a crime against humanity; and Count 8, inhumane acts as crimes against humanity. The Prosecution argues that convictions for genocide and extermination, for genocide and persecutions, for persecutions and murder, and for persecutions under Article 5 and other inhumane acts under Article 5 based on this same conduct, are not impermissibly cumulative. The second ground of appeal of the Prosecution concerns the sentence imposed by the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber erred in imposing a sentence of 46 years and that the appropriate sentence is instead life imprisonment. First, the Prosecution argues that the sentence was inadequate in light of the gravity of the offences; second, it argues that the sentence is in disparity with comparable cases decided by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda; third, that the Trial Chamber erred in basing the sentence on the fact that, in the Trial Chamber's view, Mr. Krstic's guilt was less than the guilt of other Bosnian Serb high political and military officials; finally, the Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber should have found Mr. Krstic's state of mind to be an aggravating factor in sentences. The first ground of appeal of the Defence relates to Mr. Krstic's conviction for genocide. The Defence argues that the Trial Chamber erred in finding Mr. Krstic guilty of genocide because it wrongfully equated displacement of a group with destruction of a group. The Defence also argues that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that Mr. Krstic had the necessary intent to commit genocide. Specifically, the Defence argues that the Trial Chamber's conclusion is not supported by sufficient factual bases. The second ground of appeal of the Defence concerns the discovery practices of the Prosecution. The Defence argues that those practices violated Mr. Krstic's right to a fair trial and requests a retrial. This argument has four parts: First, the Defence argues that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that the Prosecution was not bound by Rule 65 ter and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the President to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I will. Let me repeat the sentence. First, the Defence argues that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that the Prosecution was not bound by Rule 65 ter, as it then was, to disclose copies of exhibits prior to the Prosecution opening its case; second, that the non-disclosure of a tape and its subsequent playing in court prejudiced Mr. Krstic at trial; third, that the Prosecution failed to disclose to the Defence exculpatory material in accordance with the terms of Rule 68; finally, the Defence argues that the Prosecution violated Rule 68 by failing to disclose evidence relating to the investigation of two witnesses called proprio motu by the Trial Chamber. The third ground of appeal of the Defence is that the Trial Chamber erred in its findings on various factual and legal issues. The Defence argues that the Trial Chamber did not have sufficient facts to support a number of conclusions it has reached. Those conclusions relate to crimes committed in Potocari, to the alleged participation of the Bratunac Brigade in executions at Branjevo Farm and Pilica Dom, to the existence of a parallel chain of command, and to the date on which Mr. Krstic assumed command of the Drina Corps. The fourth and final ground of appeal of the Defence relates to sentencing. The Defence argues that the Trial Chamber did not sufficiently take into account the sentencing practices of Bosnia and Herzegovina since the alleged commission of the crimes and also that the Trial Chamber failed to properly take the personal circumstances of Mr. Krstic into account. I would like now to remind the parties about the criteria applicable to errors of fact or law alleged on appeal. As the Appeals Chamber has pointed out on many occasions, the appeal is not an occasion for the parties to repeat their case. This is not a de novo trial. On appeal, the parties must limit their arguments to the questions which fall within the framework of Article 25 of the Tribunal's Statute. In general, the Appeals Chamber does not hear any arguments but those founded on errors of law which allegedly would invalidate the judgement. Only exceptionally may a party raise a question of general interest for the case law of the Tribunal. As to errors of fact, only those which would have caused a miscarriage of justice will be considered. As the parties should be well aware, the Appeals Chamber requires the appellant who alleges errors of fact to demonstrate that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached the conclusion being challenged and that the error of fact is of such gravity as to produce a miscarriage of justice. I would also ask the parties to be precise and clear in their presentations of the grounds of appeal and their responses and replies. Let me now outline the precise order in which we will hear the arguments. This is the order set out in our scheduling order of 19 November 2003. We will first hear the appeal by the Prosecution. The counsel for the Prosecution will present his arguments for 1 hour and 30 minutes. We will then break for 30 minutes. Upon our return, the Defence will present its response also for 1 hour and 30 minutes. We will then break for lunch for 1 and a half hours. After lunch, the Prosecution will have 20 minutes to present its reply. At that point, we will begin the hearing of the Defence appeal. The Defence will have one hour this afternoon to commence its submissions. We will then conclude our hearing for today and resume at 9.30 a.m. tomorrow. At that point, the Defence will have another hour and 30 minutes to complete its submissions. We will then break for 30 minutes. Upon the return, the Prosecution will have 1 hour and a half hour for -- 1 hour and a half hours for its response. We will then break for 30 minutes. Upon our return, the Prosecution will have another hour to conclude its response. The Defence will then receive 30 minutes to reply. After that, Mr. Krstic, if he so chooses, may address the Appeals Chamber for 15 minutes. If there are no questions about the schedule which I have outlined - and I presume there are none - there is one matter which we have to deal with before we begin the hearing of arguments. That outstanding matter is from Friday's hearing, and we need to resolve it now. As the parties recall, on Friday the Defence moved orally to admit as additional evidence on this appeal the testimony of Mr. Richard Butler in the case of Prosecutor against Blagojevic. The Prosecution indicated that it had no objection to the motion and the Appeals Chamber granted it. I understand the Defence wishes to put Mr. Butler on the stand; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. In terms of the Prosecution appeal, the appeal will be argued by Mr. Xavier Tracol and Mr. Mathias Marcussen, who are both at the counsel table with me. If you'll excuse me, I'll just step out of the way so they can get to the podium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Tracol, we will now hear your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, President. Good morning, Judges. [In English] -- good morning. [Interpretation] Mr. President, dear Judges, the first ground of appeal of the Prosecution has to do with the fact that the Trial Chamber erroneously applied the cumulative conviction test. The Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber erred in applying the test to genocide and to crimes against humanity, on the one hand, and to persecution and other crimes against humanity, on the other hand. Let me briefly recapitulate the test as set out by the Appeals Chamber for the cumulative conviction test before demonstrating how the Trial Chamber erred in the Krstic case. The Appeals Chamber set out the test with relation to cumulative conviction test in the Delalic decision, paragraphs 412 and 413, and the same criterion or test or standard was confirmed in paragraphs 168 and 174 of the Kunarac test. It is the standard of the distinctly -- material distinct set. So the decision has to be taken on the crime presenting a distinct element. In the Krstic judgement, the Trial Chamber erred in the way it applied the test to genocide and to crimes against humanity. Let's first deal with the legal distinction between genocide and crimes against humanity. The Trial Chamber concluded in paragraph 682 of its judgement, which I'm going to quote, at the demand for an "all-out systematic attack against a civilian population under Article 5 of the Statute is included in the one, included to genocide, with the intention to destroy a specific type of group." The Prosecution quotes that in doing so the Trial Chamber erred in law inasmuch as legal elements qualify genocide and crimes against humanity. The Musema decision follows the Krstic judgement, and in that decision the ICTR Appeals Chamber decided -- found that the proof of a crime against humanity in the framework of a systematic attack against a civilian population is not demanded for genocide. In the reverse, for genocides you have to have the proof that you have the intention to destroy, all or in part, a group and -- to have a crime against humanity. Therefore, indirectly the ICTR Appeals Chamber already found in the Musema decision -- 366 and 367 of the decision -- that the elements are quite distinct. In practice, the Prosecution finds that it is possible to have a cumulative test in all cases in genocide and crimes against humanity inasmuch as each offence presents a distinct element. In the one hand, a generalised or systematic attack against the civilian population for crimes against humanity, and the intention to destroy all or in part a group as such, to have the crime of genocide. Now, dealing with the way the test is applied to the cumulative conviction test in genocide and extermination. The Trial Chamber, in paragraph 685 of the judgement, says that "On the basis of the same act it is not possible to convict somebody for both extermination and genocide." The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in law in applying the test to cumulative conviction. In this same Musema decision, the Appeals Chamber of ICTR already set out the issue and concluded with a different conclusion than the one of the Trial Chamber in the Krstic case. Three -- in paragraph 362 and 363 of the Musema decision, the ICTR Appeals Chamber applied expressly the standard set out in the Delalic case and looked at genocide and extermination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I wonder whether or not you are following too fast a pace for if interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I'm sorry. In the Musema decision, the Appeals Chamber said that the state of mind, that the intention to destroy in all or in part a group is not part of extermination. In the reverse, there is an element that is necessary for crimes against humanity; in other words, a generalised or systematic attack against the civilian population, and that element is not necessary for genocide. The ICTR Appeals Chamber concluded in paragraph 366 of the Musema decision that the element of each offence are different. It concluded that the conviction for genocide and extermination on the basis of the same conduct is possible and permissible. The Prosecution submits that we meet the Musema test and we say that the Trial Chamber erred in law in not finding General Krstic guilty of extermination. There is no reason why the Appeals Chamber should change the decision made by the Appeals Chamber in the Musema case. The Prosecution also submits that the reasoning and the conclusion of the Musema case apply to this case and this Appeals Chamber must draw the same conclusions. Therefore, the Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber did err in law by finding that an accused cannot be found guilty on the basis of the same conduct for genocide and extermination in paragraph 685 of the Krstic judgement. This is the reason why the Prosecution respectfully asks the Appeals Chamber to change the decision made as to not finding General Krstic for genocide and extermination. It asks for paragraph 685 to be revised and to find General Krstic also guilty of genocide and extermination. Let us now turn to the way the cumulative conviction test applies to genocide and persecution. The Trial Chamber, in paragraph 684 of its judgement, found that the offence of persecution does not include any element that would not already be included in the will to -- of -- or to destroy, which is demand by genocide." Therefore, the Trial Chamber did not find General Krstic guilty of persecution. In the Musema decision, the ICTR Appeals Chamber found that the elements of genocide and of crimes against humanity are markedly distinct. The decisions of the ICTR Appeals Chamber as to the distinctive elements of genocide and crimes against humanity also, therefore, apply to persecution. Therefore, this Appeals Chamber must draw the same conclusions. Based on the reasoning of the ICTR Appeals Chamber, in the Musema decision, the Appeals Chamber is bound to conclude that there is a distinctive element for prosecution as compared to genocide. Therefore, logically, the Trial Chamber erred in applying the test for multiple conviction with regard to genocide and conclusion. For the grounds already set out by the ICTR Appeals Chamber in the Musema decision, the Prosecution requires that this Appeals Chamber found that the Trial Chamber erred in finding, in paragraph 684, that only the characterisation of genocide must be held against General Krstic. We therefore ask the Appeals Chamber to annul the conclusion of the Trial Chamber, to revise paragraph 684 of the judgement, and to find General Krstic cumulatively guilty of genocide and persecution. Now, dealing with the way we apply the standard to persecution and other crimes against humanity. In paragraphs 675 and 676 of the Krstic trial judgement, the Trial Chamber found General Krstic guilty of persecution but not guilty of murder and not guilty of other inhumane acts. The Trial Chamber defined the offences and found that the offence of persecution demands an additional element, namely that the act was committed for discriminatory grounds. However, the Trial Chamber concluded without providing any explanation that murder and other inhumane acts do not require any distinct element in relation to persecution. The Appeals Chamber has never had the opportunity to rule on the general question of the cumulative conviction for persecution and other crimes against humanity; however, Trial Chambers issued judgements in relation to the issue, both before and after the Delalic decision was issued in which the Appeals Chamber set out the criteria for cumulative conviction tests. And Trial Chambers did issue rather diverging conclusions, which I'm going to set out briefly. In the Kupreskic trial judgement, Trial Chamber II found Josipovic and Vladimir Santic guilty of persecution and murder, on the one hand, and also for persecution and other inhumane acts. All the parties appealed against the judgement; however, the Appeals Chamber has not had an opportunity to rule on this issue in the Kupreskic case. The Kupreskic trial judgement was issued before the Delalic decision in which the Appeals Chamber set out the criterion relative to cumulative conviction. However, the Prosecution argues that the legal value of the trial judgement is intact inasmuch as the Trial Chamber looked into the same sources as the Appeals Chamber in the Delalic decision. You have among them the Blockberger test, which apparently was the foundation on which the Appeals Chamber rested in order to set out the test with relation to cumulative conviction. In the view of the Prosecution, the criterion of reciprocal specialty adopted and applied by the Trial Chamber in the Kupreskic case, paragraph 685, is similar and practically identical to the test that was eventually adopted by the Appeals Chamber in the Delalic decision. In the Kordic and Cerkez trial judgements, Trial Chamber III found Dario Kordic cumulatively guilty of persecution and murder based on the same conduct. It also found the two co-accused cumulatively guilty of persecution and other inhumane acts. And like the Kupreskic trial judgement, Kordic and Cerkez trial judgement was issued less than one week after the Delalic decision. In paragraphs 814 to 816 of the said trial judgement, the Trial Chamber expressively said that it relied on the test -- the cumulative-conviction test as set out by the Appeals Chamber in the Delalic decision. Neither of the two convicted people appealed against this cumulative conviction test; and therefore the judgement is final with relation to the issue. In the Kvocka trial judgement, Trial Chamber I, which was made up of exactly the same Judges as in the Krstic trial judgement, found that the crime of persecution, when dealing with the same acts committed against the same victims, cover the same -- cover the same facts. The other facts incriminated will make up crimes against humanity if they include an additional distinct element, which is that of discrimination, for one of the grounds set out above. Paragraph 220 of the Kvocka judgement, it says that murder does not include any distinction element with regard to persecution. Therefore, the Trial Chamber thought and found that the offence of persecution is more specific than murder. In the Vasiljevic trial judgement, Trial Chamber II, in paragraph 267 of its judgement, found that the Prosecution must demand the proof of a discriminatory act or intention and therefore are more specific than murder or other inhumane acts which do not require any distinct element with regard to persecution. Therefore, the Trial Chamber in the Vasiljevic case found Vasiljevic guilty of persecution but not of murder and other inhumane acts. The way the Judges reasoned was limited to the statement that persecution demands the proof of a discriminatory act or intention and that persecution is therefore more specific than other crimes against humanity. Once again, it failed to provide any explanation. It just took as a premise that murder and other inhumane acts failed to present any distinct element, with regard to persecution. Lastly, in the Naletilic and Martinovic Trial Chamber, Trial Chamber I, section 8, found in paragraph 724 of the judgement that - I quote - "When an accused person is found guilty of persecution and of another crime against humanity, the conviction to be held against him is that for persecution." I set out that we appealed against this decision by the Trial Chamber in the Naletilic and Martinovic case. As you can see, the case law as established by Trial Chambers, with relation to cumulative conviction, with a difference between persecution and other crimes against humanity, is, to say the least, incoherent. We point out this error in law by the Trial Chamber in the Krstic decision and in so doing we give the Appeals Chamber the opportunity to shed light on case law established by Trial Chambers. The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chambers which turned down a cumulative conviction for persecution and other crimes against humanity did so because they found that decision on the fact that the other crimes against humanity would fail to find or to present a distinct element to those determined in the Delalic decision. The Prosecution is bound to conclude that the conclusion -- or the finding of the Trial Chamber is erroneous. Let us look at the way the test was applied to persecution and murder. The Trial Chamber concluded in paragraph 675 of the judgement that "Murder fails to present any specific or distinct element with regard to persecution." The Prosecution submits that the finding of the Trial Chamber is an error in law. Murder is distinguishable from persecution in ways: You have to prove that the death of the victim is a result of the act of the accused; and the second element is that the intention to kill or to cause violations of -- to cause grievous bodily harm, where it can be reasonably inferred that they will lead to death. You have the constant case law of the Trial Chamber, and there's a difference with regard to murder, because it demands that there is a manifest or denial of a fundamental right consecrated by customary international law which reaches the same degree of seriousness as other crimes against humanity. And the second element which makes a distinction between murder and persecution, it is the state of mind, the discriminatory intent of the author of this act. In the Kupreskic judgement, the Trial Chamber rightly found that you need to have an element of discrimination in persecution which is not required for murder. This is paragraph 706 of the Kupreskic trial judgement. In the said judgement, the Prosecution also submits that the Trial Chamber was right in finding that a person can be accused both of murder and of persecution. Paragraph 708 of the Kupreskic judgement: The same acts causing death can then be regarded as constituent of the two offences if it is proved, first, that murder as an act of persecution meets the two conditions of discriminatory intent and generalised or systematic practice of persecution and, second condition, that murder as a crime against humanity meets both conditions of the deliberate sacrifice of the life of innocent civilians and of the generalised or systematic practice of the killing of civilians. In the Kupreskic trial judgement, the Trial Chamber therefore found that an accused can be found guilty based on the same conduct both of persecution and murder. The Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber in the Kupreskic case rightfully found that persecution and murder are distinct offences in international criminal law inasmuch as each offence is made up of a distinctively different element. In the Krstic trial judgement, the Trial Chamber therefore erred in law in finding differently and in failing to find General Krstic guilty of murder. This is the reason why the Prosecution requires or asks of the Appeals Chamber that it annuls the finding of the Trial Chamber, asked for paragraph 675 to be revised, and for General Krstic to be found guilty of persecution and murder. Let us now turn to the way the cumulative conviction test is applied to persecution in other inhumane acts. In the Krstic case, the Trial Chamber did not find General Krstic guilty of other inhumane acts because it found that other inhumane acts do not present any distinctive element that would be different with regard to persecution in the form of forced transfer. The Prosecution knows the Krnojelac decision in which, in paragraph 188, the Appeals Chamber found that the crime of persecution for inhumane acts subsumes the crime against humanity of inhumane acts, therefore making it possible to have multiple convictions on the basis of the same facts. The Prosecution, of course, also is aware of the Aleksovski decision in which the Appeals Chamber in paragraph 107 found that the adequate reading of the Statute in the light of its text as such and of its objective leads to conclude that in the interest of security and legal safety, the Appeals Chamber must follow its previous decision but is free to take out the decisions if higher decisions make it necessary in the interest of justice. Other quote from the Aleksovski decision: "In situations where in the higher interests of justice there are compelling reasons that make it necessary to change a decision compared to before, we have the example of a principle -- a legal principle of a decision that would have been issued per incurium because the Judges would have erroneously found or were not aware of the applicable law. In the Krnojelac decision, the Prosecution points out that the Appeals Chamber has examined proprio motu the notion of multiple convictions. In other words, the parties were not able to present their own arguments in their briefs on the issue. And this issue was not discussed either during the appeal hearing, so there was no pleading by the parties in writing, in the briefs filed by the parties, or in the discussions or pleadings during the hearings. This being so, the Prosecution finds that the Appeals Chamber is not really aware of the applicable law as defined in the Aleksovski decision because the parties have not had an opportunity to present their arguments but that the Appeals Chamber made a decision proprio motu. Therefore, the Prosecution concludes or finds that the paragraph 108 of the -- 188 of the Krnojelac decision was issued per incurium, as was the case, or as determined by paragraph 108 of the Aleksovski decision. In the Kunarac decision, the Chamber says that it has to set out clearly enough the grounds of its decision. In the Krnojelac decision, the Prosecution finds that the Appeals Chamber did not clearly set out its reasoning and did not present the grounds at which it based its decision, with relation to cumulative conviction, with a distinction between persecution and other inhumane acts. Therefore, paragraph 188 of the Krnojelac decision is not in keeping with the conditions set out in paragraph 42 of the Kunarac decision. This being so, the Prosecution does not see paragraph 188 of the Krnojelac decision as a final decision that settles once and for all the issue of cumulative conviction for persecution and other inhumane acts. The Prosecution believes that the Appeals Chamber is free, in the interest of justice, to make another decision than that contained in paragraph 188 of the Krnojelac decision and paragraph 108 of the Aleksovski decision. Therefore, the Prosecution maintains its ground of appeal for these issues of persecution and presents its own arguments. The Prosecution, of course, argues that the other inhumane acts and persecution meet the criterion for cumulative conviction. In the Delalic Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber found that the other inhumane acts only include the acts - and here I quote paragraph 543 - "Acts that cause great mental or physical suffering or are a violation of human dignity." This conclusion, this finding in the Delalic judgement, is in keeping with other judgements. Look at paragraph 818 of the Kupreskic trial judgement and paragraph 728 to 764 of the Tadic judgement: Mental or physical suffering or a violation of human dignity qualify the other -- or characterise the other inhumane acts. This is not a legal prerequisite for persecution. Therefore the Prosecution concludes that persecution and other inhumane acts are distinct elements. The other inhumane acts are different from persecution because you have to prove that the victim has suffered grave mental or physical suffering or a grave violation to human dignity. Once again, the crime -- or the offence of persecution does not require this element. Therefore, the Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber in the Krstic case erred in law by not finding General Krstic guilty of other inhumane acts. Therefore, the Prosecution urges the Appeals Chamber to annul the finding of the Appeals Chamber, to revise paragraph 675 of the judgement, and to find General Krstic cumulatively guilty of persecution and other inhumane acts. The Prosecution also argues that the legal distinction between persecution and other crimes against humanity is not a merely technical issue; it is also the reflection of fundamentally different legal values which are protected by every provision. In the Kunarac decision, the Appeals Chamber in paragraph 174 stressed that we should not mechanically or blindly apply principles. In the Kupreskic trial judgement, the Trial Chamber found in paragraphs 695 and 710 of the judgement that the criterion of various or different protected values confirms and corroborates the results obtained through the test of clearly distinct elements. The Prosecution also argues that the protection of various public interests is something that was recognised by Judge Shahabuddeen in his partially divergent opinion next to the Jelisic decision, paragraph 42. Judge Shahabuddeen stated that "The full protection of various public interests, as reflected in the specific elements of a crime, demands cumulative conviction." The criterion of various or different public interests is therefore an additional criterion, but it is no way a substitution to the criterion as set out by the Appeals Chamber in the Delalic case. In the first instance, with regard to public interest protected by turning persecution and murder into an offence, the Trial Chamber rightfully said in the Kupreskic case that "The prohibition of persecution protects interests, public interests, that are different from those protected by the prohibition of murder." I quote paragraph 709 of the Kupreskic trial judgement. It is clear that the fact that murder and persecution are turned into offences serves different values; the prohibition of murder aims at preventing a large-scale murder of innocent civilians. More generally, it aims at saving human life in times of armed conflict. The prohibition of persecution aims at protecting civilians from various serious forms of discrimination. Therefore, it is there to reaffirm the principle of equality between groups and human beings and to maintain its compliance. Therefore, the Prosecution agrees to analysis made by the Trial Chamber and thinks that persecution and murder, and the prohibition thereof, protects distinct public interests. The prohibition of murder protects against more direct violations of human existence; therefore, protect the lives of victims whilst -- and therefore it protects the values of human life and the respect to life. Now, let us look at the way persecution and other inhumane acts protect -- by being turned into offences, protects public interest. Blaskic, paragraph 235, finds that the authors of persecution target a human being as part of a community or a group. Persecution also concerns generally and principally the protection of the identity, of political, racial and religious groups against serious violations, and it also protects the liberty, the freedom of human beings to identify to such groups. Therefore, the group is the object of the attack and the group is also the subject of legal protection. The prohibition of persecution also protects from the discriminatory deprivation of the fundamental rights, as internationally recognised. It is a vast category comprising social, economic, and political rights; therefore, going way beyond mere attacks against a single individual. The prohibition of other inhumane acts precisely protect the physical and mental integrity and the human dignity of a person as such and not as a part or a member of a community, not as a member of a group. Other inhumane acts also protect the -- any violation of the human dignity of the victim. Therefore, the Prosecution believes that the distinct elements constituent of each offence are based on public interest that are also different for each provision. The cumulative conviction test contributes, to a large measure, to have the various public interests recognised as such, as protected by the various provisions. We have paragraph 169 of the Kunarac decision and the Appeals Chamber found that convictions make it possible to show in its entirety the criminal conduct of an accused. But does that have to be shown at the appeals level? In other words, do we need a heavier penalty when you have a same conduct violating various public interests and therefore various provisions of the Statute? Based on the constant case law of this Tribunal, this is not the case. Cumulative conviction does not automatically systematically carry with it a heavier penalty. In this instant case, the error in law by the Trial Chamber in this question of the cumulative conviction does have consequences for the penalty imposed because the Prosecution is asking for General Krstic to be found guilty of four additional counts; that is, extermination, persecution, murder, and other inhumane acts. As you said and reminded yourself, Mr. President, in the beginning of the hearing, given the fact that this same -- of General Krstic is at the basis of cumulative conviction, the Prosecution does not require an increased penalty against General Krstic on the basis of the cumulative conviction in case the Appeals Chamber would grant the Prosecution its first ground of appeal. However, the Prosecution is asking the Appeals Chamber to reverse the findings of the Trial Chamber with the -- with not finding General Krstic guilty and is asking the Appeals Chamber to find General Krstic guilty of extermination, persecution, murder, and other inhumane acts. Of course, I'm available to you for any further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Would my colleagues, the Judges, wish to ask questions now or the Prosecution would move on to argue its appeal first on the remaining questions. You have not yet touched on other grounds of appeal. Sentencing; would you like to discuss sentencing now or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution is quite willing to move to the second ground of appeal, if you so wish, Mr. President. If you have questions, of course, with regard to the first ground of appeal, I could answer them afterwards, after the ground of appeal with relation to the sentence has been presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I myself will have some questions to ask you about cumulative sentencing, but I think we would proceed by asking you first to address your other ground, namely, the question of sentencing, and then the Judges will be invited by me to address whatever questions they have about your entire argument this morning. So may I invite you to proceed to the remaining ground. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. I now give the floor to my colleague, Mathias Marcussen, who's now going to present the Prosecution's seconds ground of appeal with relation to sentencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I am going, as my colleague said, to present the Prosecution's argument on the second ground of appeal of the Prosecution. In the second ground of the appeal by the Prosecution, the Prosecution requests the Appeals Chamber to revise the sentence of 46 years' imprisonment imposed on the respondent and impose a sentence of life imprisonment in the place. At the heart of the Prosecution's second ground of appeal lies a simple proposition, which is that when an accused is convicted and found guilty as a perpetrator of 8.000 murders, the forcible transfer of 20 to 25 thousand people in circumstances where it was a reasonable, foreseeable consequence to the accused that at least dozens of people would be killed, raped, and beaten, and on top of that the accused was found to play an essential role in the commission of these crimes, then there is only one sentence available, and that is, in the words of Rule 101, "Imprisonment for a term of up to and including the remainder of the convicted person's life." The Prosecution is not just disagreeing with the sentence imposed by the Trial Chamber; the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in four different ways that we have set out in the Prosecution appeal brief. The first sub-ground of appeal, if you like, is that the Trial Chamber abused its discretion and imposed a manifestly inadequate sentence in light of the crimes committed by the respondent. The second sub-ground is that the Trial Chamber erred by not taking into consideration the sentences imposed by the Rwanda Tribunal in comparable cases. The third sub-ground is that basing the respondent's sentence on his palpably less guilt than other named and unnamed perpetrators was an error. And finally, the fourth sub-ground is that the Trial Chamber erred by considering that premeditation did not apply in the respondent's case. I'm going to address all four of these sub-grounds, but I will not go through our entire appeal brief. There's no need for that; Your Honours are familiar with it already. In particular, when I come to the sub-ground about the ICTR jurisprudence, half of our second ground of appeal in our brief is taken up with a detailed analysis of that jurisprudence, and I will not repeat all those submissions, but of course I remain available for -- for questions on these things. What I will do is simply to update that part of our arguments with the most recent jurisprudence or the jurisprudence that have come out from the Rwanda Tribunal since we filed our appeal brief. I would also note that I will reverse the order of the two last sub-grounds of appeal, so that I will address first the issue of premeditation and then the comparison between the respondent and other persons involved in the crimes after the fall of Srebrenica. So I will now turn to the first sub-ground of appeal. The Prosecution, of course, recognises that Trial Chambers have considerable discretion in sentencing matters. The Prosecution also recognised -- recognises that it has the burden to show that the Trial Chamber abused its discretion. But the Prosecution also submits that this is indeed a case where an abuse or error in the discretion has occurred in a sentencing matter. And as I stated in the beginning, the problem, in the Prosecution's submission, is fundamentally that the sentence, although a heavy sentence, is manifestly inadequate in light of the very extreme gravity of the crimes committed by the respondent and by his involvement in this -- in these crimes. As I mentioned, the victims of these crimes are numerous. The legal qualification of the conduct of the accused, in terms of the crimes, led the Trial Chamber to impose convictions for the most serious international crimes. The respondent was found guilty for genocide, to the killings -- through killings and serious bodily and mental harm; he was found guilty for crimes against humanity in the form of persecution committed through murders, cruel treatment, terrorisation of the civilian population, forcible transfer, destruction of personal property; and was found guilty of murder as a violation of the laws and customs of war. And I apologise to the translators that I'm going too fast. I will try to slow down. All these crimes are, of course, very serious, but they stand out among other -- two of them stand out among other international crimes as particularly serious. The crime of persecution has been recognised as particularly grave because of the requirement that the accused has discriminatory intent; the crime of genocide has been recognised as the international crime of crimes. Most recently the Appeals Chamber in the Rutaganda case has underlined the extreme seriousness of this crime and noted its intrinsic gravity. It is not the Prosecution's case that when an accused is found guilty of either genocide or persecution the Tribunal has to impose its highest sentence, but in the Prosecution's submission, there must be a point where these grave crimes are committed at a scale that the only -- the only sentence that can be imposed is the Tribunal's highest sentence. As I mentioned at the outset, the victims in this case were 20 to 25 thousand civilian Muslims that were transferred from Potocari. Dozens of men were killed; women were raped; and scores of civilians were beaten at Potocari. Seven to eight thousand Bosnian men were executed in massacres subsequent to these events, and the respondent played a pivotal role in these crimes. These crimes, based on the -- the Trial Chamber found that these crimes not only were of big scale but they were also particularly wicked. The Trial Chamber itself described the crimes that followed the fall of Srebrenica as one of the most heinous wartime acts committed in Europe since the Second World War. The Trial Chamber described the appalling conditions in Potocari, where there had been made no provisions for food nor water, and on top of that the Trial Chamber noted at paragraph 115 that the civilian refugees were subject to a terror campaign comprising threats, insults, lootings, burning of house, beatings, rapes, and murder, at paragraph 150. The Trial Chamber also noted the appalling conditions in which the men -- the Bosnian men that were separated out from the civilian group at Potocari was kept in at the "White House." The Trial Chamber noted -- described as an ordeal and a manhunt the shelling of the Bosnian Muslim column that tried to cross the road when they were trying to flee from Srebrenica. They described the manner in which the crimes -- the executions were carried out as "slaughter in carefully orchestrated mass executions." The executions were carried out in a manner which the Trial Chamber described as an "unspeakable evil," and it did so in reference to Erdemovic's testimony about how he pleaded with some of the executioners not to use machine-guns that would not immediately kill the victims and how other victims at other massacre sites were lying on the ground, not dead, and being left there to die slowly. So the Trial Chamber found not only massive crimes but also that there were -- many of them were executed in a particularly cruel manner. In its final findings, the Trial Chamber used words as "heinous," "indiscriminate", "disproportionate", "terrifying" to describe the crimes. It is submitted that for this reason alone the most severe punishment should be imposed on a person who has been found to have committed the crimes. The respondent, of course, did not commit the crimes himself, but he was found to have been a participant in two joint criminal enterprises, and it follows, as is well known, from the jurisprudence of the Tribunal that that means that he must be equalled to a person who has committed the crimes. Your Honours have expanded on this in the Appeals Chamber judgement in Tadic in paragraphs 191 and 192. I'm not going to repeat what Your Honours have said there. I find it worth noting, though, that in -- in the trial judgement in Stakic, Vasiljevic, and Krnojelac the Trial Chambers have stressed that "Provided the agreed crime is committed by one of the participants in a joint criminal enterprise, all the participants are equally guilty of the crime, regardless of the role they played in its commission." The most recent reference would be to paragraph 435 of Stakic, with further references there. Again, it is submitted that when an accused is found guilty to have committed crimes on this scale, the accused must be given the highest sentence. The Prosecution recognised also that when it comes to sentencing, the acts -- or the actual participation of the accused must be taken into consideration. The Prosecution submits, though, that when that is done in this case, based on the Trial Chamber's findings, it only compounds the fact that the most serious sentence must be imposed in this case. The Trial Chamber found that the respondent played a crucial role in the joint criminal enterprise that involved the forcible transfer and the genocide. With respect to the forcible transfer, the Trial Chamber found that he played a principal organising role by -- sorry, that's wrong. I'll rephrase -- I'll repeat that quote -- that he was -- that "He played a principal role in organising the buses for the evacuation throughout the day of the 12th of July." That is, that he organised the means by which the crime could be executed, the transfer. In the early morning, at 7.35, he ordered his transport officer to procure 50 buses. During the day, he checked on the progress of getting the buses to Potocari and he was -- the and Trial Chamber found that he was present in Potocari to oversee the transfer together with Mladic. The Trial Chamber concluded from the evidence that the respondent generally supervised the transportation operation. So the respondent's involvement in the transfer of the 20 to 25 [sic] civilians from Potocari was primarily a principal role. According to the Trial Chamber's findings, his involvement in the genocidal murder operation was equally important, if not even more important, because the Main Staff had no -- no real assets itself to commit the crimes with but was only an organisational shell, the respondent was -- the respondent's participation was described as indispensable - that is, Your Honours, without the respondent the crimes could not have been committed. The Prosecution has in paragraphs 410 to 417 set out in more details reference to -- references to the relevant parts of the judgements where the respondent's involvement in the executions is described by the Trial Chamber. I'll just summarise the findings. When the respondent became the commander of the Drina Corps, he knew that thousands of Muslims had been captured in his zone of responsibility. From then on, he knew that his personnel, equipment, and facilities were being used in the killing operations. The Trial Chamber specifically finds that he was aware that his assets were being used for the killing of at least 4.700 Muslim men. Those are the massacre sites at Orahovac on the 14th of July, where 1.000 people were killed; at Petkovic Dam on the 15th of July, where 1.500 to 2.000 people were killed; at Branjevo Farm, where 1.000 to 1.200 killings were taking place; at Pilica Dom, 500 people killed on the 16th; and two smaller massacre sites, at Kozluk and Nezuk. The respondent knew about these events. He was a commander of the Drina Corps and he did nothing to stop these crimes being committed within his zone of responsibility. On the 15th of July, he was directly informed by Beara that there was still 3.500 prisoners that had not been executed, and Beara asked him to assist. The respondent did not refuse. As a matter of fact, he proposed different of his units that could assist in this operation. When none of them were available, he said he would see what he could do. The Trial Chamber found that he did see what he could do and he did provide men to participate in the operation. Now, this is going to be the subject of more debate tomorrow, but the Prosecution's submission is that his involvement in all these crimes were very significant. Indeed, on the 16th of July he also provided -- ensured that there would be diesel for transportation, that there was military -- his military police was involved in escorting prisoners, and the killing at Branjevo Farm that occurred on the 16th took place at a military installation. He was apprised of these events by one of his direct subordinates, Popovic, on the 16th, and Popovic responded back to the respondent again on the 17th. So clearly he was aware of these crimes and he continued to allow his -- his troops and his equipment to be used for these operations. The Trial Chamber found in its conclusions -- in its concluding paragraphs that he participated in the full scope of the criminal plan to kill the Bosnian Muslim men, and it described his -- as I said, his involvement in these crimes as clearly indispensable. The Prosecution submits that in a case like this, where we have such big crimes, where we have an accused who's so heavily involved in the crimes, when the crimes are particularly heinous, there is only one sentence available and that is life imprisonment and that the Trial Chamber, by not imposing that sentence, abused its discretion in this case. I'll briefly address the Prosecution's second sub-ground of appeal. As I mentioned, I'm not going to go through all our submissions on the Rwanda jurisprudence, but if you have any questions, I'm of course available. What I'd like to note is that since our appeal brief was written, the ICTR have issued five judgements. There are two appeal judgements in Musema and Rutaganda. Essentially -- well, not essentially. These judgements confirm the sentences imposed on Musema and Rutaganda, so therefore they do not change anything for our argument. And I think that's just an important point to note. There are three Trial Chamber judgements that have come out this year in the spring, in the case of Elizaphan and Gerard Ntakirutimana in the Semanza case and in the Niyitegeka case. Elizaphan Ntakirutimana was imposed a prison sentence of ten years. His case is distinguished -- excuse me, is distinguishable from the case at hand and from the other cases that we have referred to in our appeal brief in that Elizaphan Ntakirutimana was found to be an aider and abettor, and it was found that there were mitigating circumstances in his case that outweighed the aggravating circumstances. His case is therefore not comparable to the -- to that of the respondent's. Gerard Ntakirutimana was convicted for genocide and given a sentence of 25 years' imprisonment. In his case, the aggravating factors were found to outweigh the mitigating factors. In that sense, this judgement could be said to have an impact on the Prosecution's argument in the appeal brief. However, the Prosecution notes that Gerard Ntakirutimana was found guilty of only two murders as the act of genocide, and therefore, again, this case cannot be compared with that of the respondent's. Semanza was sentenced for a number of crimes, among them genocide, for which he was sentenced to a term of five years of imprisonment -- excuse me, he was -- five years of imprisonment for complicity in genocide. And because he was found guilty for complicity in genocide and the Trial Chamber in that case considered that that would lead to a lower sentence, again, this case does not do much in terms of having impact on the Prosecution's submission and the appeal brief. Finally, in the Niyitegeka case, I would submit that that case also does little to our appeal brief. Niyitegeka was found guilty of genocide. He was given a term of life imprisonment. And that whole judgement is in line with the other judgements where -- where senior officials have been involved in crimes in Rwanda. We're not relying on this case as further support for the argument we have made, but I thought I should bring these -- this case to your attention as well. I should also mention that all these cases are subject to appeal. So for the reasons that we have set out in our appeal brief, we submit that the Trial Chamber erred when it did not take into account the sentencing practice of the Rwanda Tribunal. It's our submission that the sentencing practice is relevant also to this Tribunal because although the crimes in Rwanda happened in very different circumstances, we're still talking about international -- the international crimes of genocide and crimes against humanity, and in the clear sentencing practice of Rwanda those who are responsible for these crimes at -- at least when they took place, at a -- at a big level, on a big scale and where the accused holds a position of authority, then the sentences being imposed are the Tribunal's most severe sentence, life imprisonment. So we submit that had the Trial Chamber had due regard to this sentencing practice, it would have imposed a life sentence. I now turn to our fourth sub-ground in the brief and, of course, my third point. It concerns the finding in paragraph 712 of the judgement. There the Trial Chamber agrees with the Prosecution that premeditation is relevant as an aggravating factor in the abstract, but then it says, "based on the sequence of General Krstic's delayed participation in the genocidal scheme initiated by General Mladic and others," it finds that it is not applicable to this situation. The Prosecution submit that is the Trial Chamber thereby erred in law. The jurisprudence of the Trial shows that planned and calculated submissions of crimes warrant the application of premeditation as an aggravating circumstance. In Celebici, the Trial Chamber held that "where an accused is found to have committed offences charged with cold, calculated premeditation suggestive of revenge against the individual victim or the group to which the victim belongs, such circumstances necessitates the imposition of aggravating punishment." The ICTR have defined premeditation in relation to murder as the acts as formulated -- that the acts are formulated the intent to kill after a cool moment of reflection." Black's Law Dictionary states that "Premeditation involves a design or a plan to commit a crime before it's committed." In our appeal brief paragraphs 4117 and 4118, we refer to more domestic legislation and jurisprudence on premeditation, but I'm not going to go through that here. What I'd like to stress, with respect to the aspect of premeditation which concern a plan to commit a crime is that it is sufficient that the accused know about the plan, he adopts it and executes it. It's not a requirement that the accused, him or herself, makes the plan. We've cited in our appeal brief as an example R. versus Brown from Canada. There's more on that in paragraph 4122 of our appeal brief. As examples of premeditation in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal could be mentioned the destruction of a mosque that could only have taken -- that only could have been carried out by an expert who knew exactly where to have placed explosives, in Blaskic, paragraph 421; or a terrorist attack on a lorry that was found to be premeditated because it was necessary to arrange considerable -- considerable quantities of explosives, organise the transport of the booby-trapped vehicle, and plan where to place it; again, Blaskic paragraph 505. In Celebici, it was found that when the accused inflicted burns on a detainee, it would have been premeditated. And also in Celebici, warning a victim before beating him that he should not hope to be alive was considered evidence of premeditation. In his response brief, the respondent has suggested that premeditation would necessarily encapsulate the elements of genocide and crimes against humanity and therefore cannot be an aggravating factor when such crimes are committed. The Prosecution submits that that argument should be rejected and refer to the case of Serushago from the Rwanda Tribunal, which did consider premeditation an aggravating circumstance in sentencing Serushago for both crimes against humanity and genocide. And that sentence was upheld by the Appeals Chamber. The Prosecution submits that in light of the legal principles that I've just outlined, the Trial Chamber erred in two ways: First, it only considered premeditation in relation to the joint criminal enterprise to commit genocide but did not consider whether there was premeditation in relation to Potocari; and second, it -- it ignored its previous findings with respect to how the genocidal events occurred and failed to draw the correct legal inferences from that, namely, that the respondent's participation in the crimes were premeditated. The Prosecution would submit, with respect to Potocari, that the events that I've already described, of organising buses throughout the whole day constitute premeditation. Clearly the respondent would have had time to reflect upon what he was doing. He, as a matter of fact, thought about how this crime should be carried out and ordered one of his subordinates to take steps. He then followed up and supervised. In the Prosecution's respectful submission, that is -- those acts are -- can only be described as premeditated. With respect to the events that involve the execution of the Bosnian Muslim men, I've also described how the respondent was heavily involved all through the execution of these crimes. As a commander of the Drina Corps, from the evening of the -- or the late afternoon of the 13th of July, he was informed about what was happening; he allowed his assets to be used; he was asked for assistance; he provided assistance. There can be only one inference from these fact, according to the Prosecution, and that is that he participated in the plan to execute the men. He knew of the plan; he participated in it. As I mentioned in the beginning, that would constitute, on its own, premeditation. But secondly, each of these acts before each contribution by the respondent, he would have ample time to consider what he was doing. He chose to go along with the plan. He chose to lend his assistance. That, in the Prosecution's submission, constitutes premeditation. For those reasons, Your Honours, we submit that the Trial Chamber was in error when it did not apply as an aggravating circumstance in this case premeditation. The Prosecution also respectfully submits that had the Trial Chamber applied this aggravating circumstance, it could only have come to one conclusion. When this aggravating circumstance was add to the other aggravating circumstances found by the Trial Chamber, and taking into consideration the scale of the crime, the heinous nature of the crimes, the degree of the respondent's participation, the Trial Chamber would have had to come to the conclusion that the respondent should be given a life sentence. So again, for this reason alone, the Appeals Chamber is respectfully requested to revise the sentence of the respondent. And finally, I'll turn to our third sub-ground of appeal in our brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, I think that we are to respect the break for the interpreters. How long do you have to -- would you like to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I can finish this in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Let me ask the interpreters, they could continue for five more minutes, the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you for your cooperation. So five more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I apologise to the interpreters. Your Honours, to make it short, the Prosecution submits that in paragraph 724 the Trial Chamber erred by comparing the -- the involvement of the respondent to Mladic and other -- the involvement of Mladic and other unnamed persons that were also involved in these crimes. The Prosecution submits that although the trial -- the Appeals Chamber has held that it's important that there is a principle of gradation of sentencing, there comes a point where the crimes are so grave that this gradation has to be set aside. One has to look at the conduct of the accused and if his conduct is sufficiently important and his crimes sufficiently grave, the right sentence is the life sentence. It's the only sentence. And it does not matter whether there are others who were also involved in those crimes or in other crimes in the same conflict that could be said to be morally or legally more responsible. I've repeatedly stated how important we think it is that one considers the large scale of the crime, the heinous nature of the crime, and the respondent's very, very important involvement in the crime, according to the Trial Chamber's own finding. I'm tempted to repeat - and I will give in to my temptation - the respondent was found to be indispensable in the commission of the genocide. Again, without him - that would be the conclusion - without him, these crimes could not have been committed. He was clearly also extremely important in the events at Potocari, because he organised the buses. He was the person who could organise the buses, organise the means by which the crime could be committed, the forcible transfer. The Prosecution recognises, as I said, that this means that people who were even more involved would be given the same -- the same sentence as the respondent. But this, Your Honours, is not unknown in criminal law. As a matter of fact, in most, if not all, domestic jurisdictions, if an accused is found guilty of five murders, he will be given the highest sentence, and so will the accused who's found guilty of 15, 10, or 100. There comes a point where the highest sentence is the only appropriate one. In this case, we have 7.000 people killed, 25.000 people forcibly transferred, and dozens killed, raped, and brutalised as a reasonable, foreseeable consequence of the scheme that was put in place to carry out the forcible transfer. The respondent was an important part of these crimes, and he must be given the highest sentence. I think, Your Honours, that the rest is in our brief. And in light of the need for the interpreters to have a well-deserved break, I will conclude my submissions by simply repeating that the Prosecution requests respectfully the Appeals Chamber to impose a sentence on the respondent of life imprisonment, and I'd also like to note - I would have made submissions of this at the end - that we request a minimum sentence of 30 years. Your Honours, I think I will conclude with this. We will conclude the Prosecution's appeal, unless Your Honours have questions now. But I guess we might take them after the interpreters have had a chance to rest a bit. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marcussen, for concluding your argument. Let me just explain to the counsel how we are going to proceed. We will have a 30-minute break, which means that we will resume at 11.50, at which time we will first have questions from the Bench and then turn to the distinguished counsel for the Defence to start with his response. So the Court will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Do I understand that the Prosecution is asking to speak?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. I just, with your Court's indulgence, would like to add one small thing to our submissions. I might have wrapped up leaving one point out that I should have made. I simply wanted to put on record that if the Appeals -- if the Appeals Chamber accepts the -- as reliable evidence some or all of the evidence that has been added to the appeals record and if the Appeals Chamber would come to the conclusion that this evidence changes the nature or the degree of the respondent's participation in the crimes, it would be our submission that that evidence could also affect the sentence. So I simply wanted to make that point clear. And I'm not going to make submissions on how this could affect the sentence, but of course this evidence would be subject to debate tomorrow and depending on what your ultimate decision on this would be, it's our position that it might be taken into consideration also when it comes to the sentence. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marcussen. I think that we would be ready now to -- to turn to the Judges and allow them to ask questions. If my colleagues are agreeable, I would lead off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: My first question would be to -- I have a question about sentencing, so I will turn to Mr. Marcussen on that. And then I will have, after your response -- we will see whether the Judges would like to ask you on sentencing, and then we will return to the question of cumulative convictions to Ground 1. Okay. On the sentencing. In your appeal, you have asked the Appeals Chamber to impose a life sentence with a minimum term of 30 years to take into account the possibility that Mr. Krstic might be granted an early release. You will recall that the Trial Chamber sentenced Mr. Krstic to 46 years. Assuming that he may be eligible for an early release, after serving, as it is customary, two-thirds of his sentence, this would mean that under the sentence pronounced by the Trial Chamber he would be required to serve a minimum term of just over 30 years. Can you tell me, Mr. Farrell -- Mr. Marcussen, therefore, what is the practical difference between what the Prosecution is asking in its appeal and the sentence that was actually imposed on Mr. Krstic by the Trial Chamber, because the terms of effective imprisonment would be more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours -- Your Honour. The Prosecution has appealed against the sentence and requested a sentence of life imprisonment, because we submit that that is the only appropriate sentence. And depending on how the respondent is going to serve his sentence, he might end up actually serving his full life sentence. So we are -- but that will depend on the country in which the respondent will serve his sentence; it will depend on whether a recommendation made by that country, that he might be released earlier. So that -- the regime of the country where he go, we don't know about at this stage. But by asking for a life sentence, the Prosecution is asking primarily that the respondent is sentenced to be serving the rest of his life in prison. But to ensure that he at least serve what we consider a minimum acceptable sentence, he should serve 30 years. But we are seeking an increase of the sentence, if that answers your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marcussen. Would my colleagues wish to ask questions on sentencing? Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, I gather that your position is that, in principle, it is difficult to conceive of any case in which a life sentence would be appropriate if it's not this case, that is, assuming that the convictions are maintained. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, could you tell me -- maybe I should have read it somewhere - and I apologise for not having done my homework, if it does exist somewhere - but has there been any discussion within the Tribunal of the legality of a Chamber recommending a minimum period of imprisonment? Under the Statute, Article 27 of the Statute says this: "Such imprisonment shall be in accordance with the applicable law of the state concerned subject to the supervision of the International Tribunal." Now, would that mean that if a man is sent to a given state and he's ordered to be imprisoned for life, that the state has the competence to say what is the minimum period after which he is eligible for release, subject, of course, to the supervision of the Tribunal? Could there be a conflict there? My mind is completely open on the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- there have been two instances where minimum sentences have, as a matter of fact, been imposed by the Tribunal; one is in Tadic, and that was upheld by the Appeals Chamber, and recently in Stakic. But I understand that your question is a practical one: How does this actually work out when the convicted person is sent to serve a sentence in a country? My answer would be that the minimum sentence would be binding on the state where the person is going to serve his sentence. If it is not possible for the receiving states to have a person serve the minimum sentence of 30 years for some legal reasons in that jurisdiction, that state must decline to take the respondent to serve his sentence. I think that must be the only solution available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I thank Judge Shahabuddeen. On sentencing and other questions, no. So we turn to cumulative convictions. I believe that you, Judge Shahabuddeen, had something that you wanted to raise about cumulative convictions. Why don't we start from your end and we will follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tracol - I beg your pardon - I am focussing on that part of your submissions which was directed to the permissibility of having cumulative convictions in respect of murder and persecution. I know you spoke of other things as well. The criteria have been set in previous cases. As I understand the criteria, it is this, that the test is whether one crime is subsumed in the other crime, and that depends on whether Crime A has an element not possessed by Crime B and whether Crime B has an element not possessed by Crime A. Now, looking at Article 5(h) of the Statute relating to persecutions, I wonder if it could be said that that Article -- that provision is in a sense referential. It refers the reader to certain other acts, certain crimes or certain acts which amount to persecution. Now, if that is so, then we have this: The Prosecutor has an option to refer to the conduct involved either by reference to the facts involved or be reference to legal characterisation of those facts. In this case, I see that a man is charged -- Count 6, paragraph 31 of the indictment says he's charged with the crime of persecutions, relating to, A, the murder of thousands of Bosnians, and so on. So it looks to me that a question could be asked this way: On the indictment thus framed, to establish the asserted charge of persecutions, do you have to prove each and every element of the crime of murder to which the persecution alleged in the indictment relates so that you come to this conclusion: If the man is found guilty of persecution, you would also have proven every element of the crime of murder, with reference to which the persecution is asserted? Now, if that is correct - if that is correct - does there remain any element of the crime of murder which has not been subsumed in the charge of persecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Judge, Mr. President, Your Honours, as was stated by Judge Shahabuddeen, the criterion is indeed that of the distinctly -- distinct elements for each crime in the Statute. The case law of this Tribunal - and in this respect the Prosecution follows the case law of the Tribunal - and this case law has always been to take into account the crimes as such and not the specific forms in which the crimes are presented, in order to apply the cumulative-conviction test. With regard to the crimes in question -- persecution and murder -- the Appeals Chamber must therefore apply the test, the cumulative-conviction test, to persecution and murder but not take into account the forms in which the crime of persecution was set out in the indictment. As you stressed yourself, Judge Shahabuddeen, Count 6 of the indictment takes indeed various forms; murder is one of them, but it is not the only form in which persecution can take place. The same goes for the entire case law of this Tribunal. Persecution or persecutions; it is not just murder plus discriminatory intent or the discriminatory intent of the author of the persecution. You also referred to the proof of the ingredients and elements of each crime. This is a different question, in my view, from the question of the way the cumulative-conviction test should be applied. Indeed, you can have various forms of persecution, including murder. And we will have to prove that there has been murder in this case. But this is not the way of the case law of this Tribunal - and also, the Prosecution sees the way the test should be applied. I hope I answered your question. If this is not the case, I'm, of course, available to you for further answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tracol. You have assisted me. What I have in mind is this: That paragraph 29 of that same count in the indictment refers to certain previous paragraphs of the indictment - 11, 22 through 26 - and when you consult those paragraphs, they clearly refer to executions. You see that in 22, 23, 24 -- 24.6 and so on, right down through 26. What I have in mind: Is it possible to argue that the indictment on persecution has been so constructed that it relates not merely to the physical conduct, as it were, of the accused but to his having committed murder in respect of these various and manifold executions, so that murder would be subsumed in persecutions, would form a complete part of persecution? And therefore, would there remain any element of murder which would not be comprehended by the charge of persecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my answer will be simple, even simplistic. The Office of the Prosecutor decided to charge General Krstic with persecution, including in the form of murder, but also for murder as a crime against humanity. If the Office of the Prosecutor had intended to subsume murder into a wider crime of persecution, it would not have added a distinct count of murder, it would merely have mentioned murder as one of the manifold forms of the count of persecution. But this is not the position taken by the Office of the Prosecutor, since according to the Office of the Prosecutor you have distinct elements for persecution and murder. And persecution can indeed take the form of another crime against humanity; for instance, murder, in this case, but can also not take the shape or form of a murder. Persecutions can also take the form of a crime that is not specifically mentioned in the Statute; I have in mind abuse. And this goes to show that the ingredients of these two offences are materially distinct elements. I hope I have answered your questions, once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One last point. I'm only trying to educate myself as to the nature of your case, and I'm not putting to you any preconceived position. Would I be correct, then, in understanding your reply to me to be this: That, well, in respect of murder he is not charged with murder simpliciter but murder as a crime against humanity and that involves the various elements of a crime against humanity which are not comprehended in persecution? But isn't persecutions itself a crime against humanity?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would need to answer your question to go back to the intent of the legislator, of the law-maker, who in this very instance was the Security Council. The Tribunal only has to apply the Statute and its provisions. The Article 5, in relation to crimes against humanity, comprises persecution with a -- a discriminatory element, which is very clear the way it is stated under Article 5(H) of the Statute. The Statute also comprises among crimes against humanity murder, and the way the Office of the Prosecutor interprets and reads this is that by making these two elements offences the law-maker, wanted to protect various public interests and wanted them to be reflected in the fact that such acts are criminalised with regard to the acts of the accused. This is why the Tribunal has to implement the Statute, and I do believe that the elements of these two offences are distinct elements, because in murder there is the death of the victim; persecutions do not necessarily mean that the victims are going to be killed. They don't necessarily amount to a murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tracol. I'm obliged to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you very much, Judge Shahabuddeen. Before turning to my question, if I may just, with regard to the exchange that has taken place, say only this: Yes, the intent of the legislator surely is cardinal for our work; but the intent of the legislator is not always all that clear, and it is -- this explains why the Tribunal had to resort to interpreting the intent of the legislator, and it did so by developing its fairly complex and sophisticated jurisprudence on cumulative convictions. So just to mention the intent of the legislator is not, I would suggest, all that helpful. Now, I would like to ask still on this question of cumulative conviction, I would like to turn to another aspect of the pairing of offences, that involving genocide and extermination. I would benefit from your help on how to define actus reus for genocide in comparison for -- to actus reus for extermination. The Statute speaks of -- describing the prohibited act as killing, as you know, members of the group. We are talking about certain protected groups.
