Now, does the word "members" imply some kind of a minimal number of people that one must murder to commit genocide? Is there a numerical threshold there? And how would that compare with the actus reus for extermination? That's my first question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, first of all, with regard to the actus reus of genocide, if you read the Statute and Article 4, there are many ways in which you can commit genocide. Murder is one of the ways in which it can be done. But it is, if you read the Statute - and therefore, from a strictly theoretical point of view - it's not the only way genocide can be committed according to the Statute. For instance, you can try -- that you can try to prevent the birth of members of a group. I forgot the exact wording. I'm sorry. I'm looking at the Statute. These are measures destined to prevent births.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: My question was -- referred exclusively to paragraph 2(a) of Article 4, killing members of the group. There's no need for you to complicate the matter further by discussing other aspects of Article 4, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm so sorry, Mr. President. Indeed, I had failed to read your question properly. With regard to genocide as committed through murder, the Tribunal, including the Appeals Chamber, has already set out the issue in the Jelisic case. It appears from the Jelisic case, both from the trial judgement as well as the appeals decision the murder of a single victim is enough to constitute genocide, as long as the accused had the mens rea to destroy all or part of a protected group. It is quite a -- an essential difference with regard to extermination, where the actus reus also includes a contextual element. Indeed, the case law in the ICTY and in the ICTR says that the murder must be committed in a context of a mass murder. Context; I underline that. It doesn't mean that a person accused of extermination must necessarily have committed the murder of a large number of victims. It is easily conceivable that an accused kills one single victim in the global context of mass murder and that a Chamber would find this act to be extermination. At any rate, you need to have a murder of at least one victim in both cases, as decided by the Jelisic decision for genocide but also for extermination, even if the single murder, in theory, at least, has to have taken place in the context of mass murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could you say something a little bit more about this context of mass murder for extermination, then. What would be required in order for a single murder to be -- to be regarded as part of extermination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, in my view, it all depends in the way the offence has been committed. As applied at least in this Tribunal of the notion of the joint criminal enterprise, an accused must be associated to a joint criminal enterprise intent on committing extermination or genocide by killing one victim - even if he, as such, does not kill a large number of people. However, the accused will be seen as identified or associated as other authors of the genocide or the extermination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you one more question: If you look at pages 240, 241, and specifically at footnote 1455 - 1455 - of the judgement of the Trial Chamber, you will see that the Trial Chamber drew on the International Criminal Court and it defined genocide as a prohibited conduct which, and I quote, "took place in the context of a manifest pattern of similar conduct." And this is, of course, not stated, as we all know, in the Statute of the ICC; it is something which is stated in the elements of crimes adopted by the ICC preparatory commission. Do you believe that this definition, which appeared as I cited it, in the -- has reflected customary law at the time when Mr. Krstic's conduct in question took place? If not, would it be appropriate for us to follow this statement which is included in elements of crimes? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution believes that the Trial Chamber erred in granting so much importance, and especially in giving the legal value that it did to the Rome Statute in the judgement. The Rome Statute, which created the ICC, does indeed allow to determine the opinio juris of the states, at the time the Rome Statute was adopted; in other words, 1998. At least two Trial Chambers in the case law so far established have concluded, as such, the Rome Statute is not valued as international customary law. This is paragraph 227 of the Furundzija trial judgement and footnote 1210 of the Kunarac trial judgement. As I stated earlier on, the Rome Statute was adopted in 1998, that is, following the crimes committed by General Krstic in Srebrenica; they were submitted in 1995. It is, therefore, not possible to conceive that the Rome Statute would be part and parcel of international law as applicable in 1995. I repeat it: The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in defining extermination, in finding what it found in paragraph 502 of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Guney, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just one thing for you to be able to clarify your views. The Rome Statute is the work of the progressive development and of international customary law the way it is being codified as time goes by. So if you look at the law, as it is provisionally developed -- of course, the Statute is not part and parcel of the international customary law; however, with regard to the provisions related to the progressive development of law, the Statute is part, is an integral part of international customary law.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Guney, for giving me the opportunity to clarify our position with regard to this issue. The Rome Statute is indeed a part of international law, ever since it was adopted in 1998. But as to its value as part of international customary law, I do not believe that it can be applied retroactively to the facts of this case, to crimes committed back in 1995. Indeed, the Rome Statute makes it possible for you to be guided in the way you apply international humanitarian law. It is progress, indeed, in international criminal law; however, the Rome Statute cannot be applied to this Tribunal. Of course, it can be applied to the International Criminal Court, but with regard to this Tribunal the Rome Statute can only be seen as a guidance. It cannot be applied retroactively to facts that took place in 1995, whilst the Rome Statute was adopted in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, Mr. Farrell would like to take the floor on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The issue of the interpretation of the Rome Statute and its relevance of international customary law is one of the issues that's arisen from Mr. President's question. The specific question about whether or not the context and the pattern of conduct is actually required under international customary law, as opposed to -- which will be part of my submission tomorrow, that it was adopted in the circumstances of the ICC Statute -- will be something that I will address tomorrow, if it that will be sufficient, as it relates to the genocide issue, if that may assist the Court in any way. Thank you, Mr. Farrell, and that would be perfectly agreeable that this -- you would address this question tomorrow. And I am grateful that you have specified that actually my question was very, very concrete, not Statute of the ICC in general but only the particular definition with regard to genocide requiring a manifest pattern of similar conduct. And let me further specify that even this very specific language does not appear in the Statute of the ICC but only in the elements of crimes which were adopted by the preparatory commission of the ICC subsequent to the adoption of the Statute. So let's just have this very clear, and we will return to this tomorrow. Now, we will now finally turn to the distinguished counsel for the Defence, and we are, of course -- the Bench is very well aware of the fact that he is starting his argument considerably later than we have envisaged. And let me assure him that we will recalculate the time allowed to him accordingly. And this afternoon I will give further specification regarding the exact timetable with regard to argument of the parties. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So we would ask you now to start your argument. And we will -- you will now start with your response, and you will have now until 1 hour and 15 minutes, which is 45 minutes for your argument before the lunch break. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and may it please the members of this Honourable Chamber. Incidentally, I have a feeling that I will be through with the argument by 1.15 at -- barring that that doesn't take into account the questions from the Court. But I think certainly my formal presentation will be finished by then. I'd like to start, with Your Honours' permission, on the sentencing issue. Mr. Marcussen at the beginning of his comments - I think I'm quoting him correctly - said that "When you have the murders of some 7 to 8 thousand Bosnian Muslim men coupled with the deportation forcible transfer of some 25.000 elderly men, women and children, coupled with the crimes, the foreseeable crimes, that took place at Potocari during 12 July -- 12 and 13 July 1995, it is - and I quote Mr. Marcussen - "a simple proposition for the Trial Chamber to have decided that the only recourse, the only possible sentence here, given that set of facts, was a life sentence." Mr. Marcussen made the same point in effect when he was talking about how we cannot look at comparative guilt, we cannot look at the extra sense of guilt of General Mladic [sic], when he said, and I quote, he said, "Gradations must be set aside," - if I'm quoting Mr. Marcussen correctly. I'm sure I am - "Gradations must be set aside when the crime is as heinous as this one." I think that the Trial Chamber in one paragraph has answered what Mr. Marcussen's position apparently is, and that's in paragraph 700, when the Trial Chamber said "Genocide embodies a horrendous concept indeed, but a close look at the myriad of situations that can come within its boundaries cautions against prescribing a monolithic punishment for one and all genocides or similarly for one and all crimes against humanity or war crimes." That seems to me to make such eminently good sense; again, not to be absolutist about it, we seem to be absolutist today. But it makes eminently good sense to me. This really is -- this is what the Trial Chamber is all about, applying discretion and making judgements after seeing a mass of evidence and hearing witnesses and that kind of thing. And then the Trial Chamber in the Kunarac case I also think had a very wise thing to say, when it said, "The Trial Chamber considers it wrong to revert to some abstract comparison of the per se gravity of the crimes." So what the Trial Chamber did in this case - and of course, we think they were wrong in certain respects - but what the Trial Chamber did in this case was assess all of the evidence and make a very reasoned judgement as to what the sentence should be. We believe, contrary to what the Prosecution is claiming, that the conduct of General Krstic at this case is at the very bottom end of the spectrum of culpability. We believe that the three main sets of crimes that are involved here show his lack of premeditation and show that he was indeed not indispensable to the commission of any of these crimes. And I'd like to briefly discuss three sets of crimes involved in this case. We're talking about forcible transfer first; we're talking about crimes at Potocari second; and we're talking about the killings of the Bosnian Muslim men last. Starting with the forcible transfer, there's no evidence that General Krstic was involved in the -- in the organisation of this. It wasn't his idea. He didn't plan it. He just happened to be there. As of July 12th, 1995, there was this meeting at the Fontana Hotel, the Chamber -- the Judges will recall from Mr. Deronjic's testimony. And Mr. Deronjic showed up at that meeting and he said there are three options for the civilians; they can go, they can stay or they could go to another country. Of course the third option was not practical. Mr. Deronjic said -- but, you know, this was really a smoke screen. We now know, indeed, it was a smoke screen. But Mr. Deronjic had been interviewed a number of times prior to that. Your Honours will recall that we tried to get his statements admitted in our Rule 115 motion, and we also claimed it was a Rule 68 violation for the Prosecution not to have turned that over to us, because certainly on the face of the interviews it looked like a voluntary transfer, and we were critical of the Prosecution not turning over the statement to us. At least in the sense if you would accept what Mr. Deronjic said, if you would accept what he said, then the citizens had an option whether to stay or to leave. In any event, we were turned down obviously in our Rule 115 motion, but my point now is we all recognise that it was a smoke screen. We're not contesting that in this case. It was indeed a smoke screen, because when he was presenting that, he was interrupted by General Mladic - and for reasons Your Honours know all about - General Mladic, in his bullying-and-not-brooking-any-interference way, said words to the effect, you know, "You can either face death or you can go." So that was the -- that was the situation. Now, can this be attributable to General Krstic? No. Did General Krstic -- is there any evidence indicating that General Krstic knew that this was a smoke screen? Is there any evidence indicating that he shared in any way, shape, or form the kind of -- the rigidity and the cruelty that General Mladic was -- was using here? The answer again is no. So what did General Krstic do? He took part in the bussing operation; yes, he did organise the buses. Now, how indispensable was that? That was a mechanical operation -- he was -- by the way, he was not the corps commander then, he was the deputy corps commander.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise to the interpreters. He was the deputy corps commander. Anyone, I respectfully suggest, could have organised the buses. It was really a mechanical thing to do. And under those circumstances, the only humane thing to do was indeed to organise the bussing operation. If the civilians were truly facing death, if they didn't leave, for goodness sakes, the first thing you have to do is get them away, get them to safety, get them out of harm's way. And General Krstic, of course - we know this now - said, "Make sure not a hair on their head be harmed." And that was consistent with the humanitarian attitude he'd had all his life. And I'm not going to repeat it - we've set this forth in our briefs - all his life toward Bosnian Muslims or indeed any other people. And it was -- it was also events later on in the Zepa operation where he was so concerned about it that he said, "If anyone interferes with the peaceful transfer of civilians at Zepa, they'll be shot. I want absolutely nothing to interfere with the safety of these civilians." So again, General Krstic was involved in this at the last minute, after it became evident that General Mladic intended a forcible transfer. True, he learned it at that time; he did take part in it; but he did all he could to guarantee that it was a safe and peaceful transfer of civilians. I would suggest that puts him toward the bottom end of the spectrum of culpability here and not the top end. The crimes at Potocari - that's the second area we're talking about now - there were murders and other violent acts, rapes, beatings, property destruction on July 12th and 13th, 1995, while the civilians were gathered there. And we went into this in some detail in our brief, and it's very clear, as the Trial Chamber stated that, there is virtually no evidence indicating that members of the Drina Corps took part in any of these murders or beatings or rape, no evidence. There was one tiny bit of evidence, which I think the Trial Chamber said was essentially discredited. These crimes were committed by these paramilitary groups and other groups who had come into the area, not by members of the Drina Corps. And you'll recall the letter that Mr. Petrusic showed to Mr. Deronjic the other day at the -- at the additional evidence hearing, the letter of July 9th, 1995 by Major General Tolimir, citing instructions by President Karadzic that civilians were to be well treated, that kind of thing. Their property was not to be destroyed - this is OTP Exhibit 432 at the Krstic trial - and the civilian population were to be treated and war prisoners indeed were to be treated in accordance with the Geneva Convention. So why was General Krstic convicted of the crimes at Potocari? He was convicted at the crimes of Potocari because he was found to be a member of a joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer the civilians. That indeed is the case. And it is a -- under the law of the Tribunal, if killings or violent acts are -- objectively speaking, are a naturally foreseeable consequence of being a member of that enterprise, and if the actor, speaking subjectively, knew that a -- it was a possible consequence, that alone is sufficient under Tribunal law to result in a conviction. It's, from the point of view of a defendant, Your Honours, it's a very difficult standard of legal liability. I recognise with total respect that that is indeed the standard in this Tribunal. But General Krstic was convicted of these other crimes not because he took part in them in any way. He advised -- he said, "Don't touch the civilians." He did everything he could. He announced it on several occasions that no one should be harmed. And we've set this forth in the brief. Even Erdemovic, the -- one of the -- one of the murderers, one of the executioners at Branjevo Farm, testified at the trial, "Yes, at Potocari, during that period, 12/13 July, we were told not to touch the civilians." But the civilians were touched. But, again, General Krstic did his best to make sure that they were treated correctly. And it's ironic that, you know, he was not the corps commander during that period; he was the deputy corps commander on 12 and 13 July 1995, and -- and also he -- the fact that he kept trying to do the right thing under the Tribunal law, is evidence that he knew that it was possible that such terrible acts should take place. So in effect, he was -- and I say this -- I say this not -- I do say it indeed ironically -- he's furnishing evidence against himself under the -- under the Tribunal rationale by, again, making these efforts to make sure that no bad things would occur, he's -- for legal purposes, he's conceding that he knew it was possible that these things could occur. But, certainly, there was no evil intent here. The only evil intent, if we can call it that, is he did indeed take part in a -- in a joint criminal enterprise to -- to transfer the civilians., but that's it. Anything else that happened after that with was, I'm sure, as repugnant to him as any other civilised person. And finally, the third area of responsibility, the third area of culpability, are the killings of the Bosnian Muslim men. Now, these killings took place between 13 and 19 July 1995. Now, the fact is that General Krstic did not become the -- the corps commander, at least in fact, until 13 July 1995, and we're accepting what the Trial Chamber found on this issue. We had a different contention at the trial, as Your Honours know; we claimed that he didn't become the corps commander until the 20th. But let's accept the finding of the Trial Chamber; he became corps commander de facto on the 13th of July and de jure on the -- on the 15th of July. It's undisputed that on the evening of July 11th General Krstic was appointed by General Mladic to head and to take charge of the military operation in Zepa and to establish a new command post there. And from that time on, from the evening of July 11 on, with the exception of one or two hours that he was in Potocari on July 12th - this is all citing findings from the Trial Chamber now - he was more or less continually at the Zepa command post. And I believe that the -- you'll recall the testimony that was quoted from Mr. Obrenovic to the effect that when he called General Krstic at the Krivace, at the Zepa command post, on July 15th to tell him about the terrible situation that resulted from the escape of the Bosnian Muslim men, the column and the pitched battle and the furious battle that was taking place there, General Krstic, according to Mr. Obrenovic, really didn't seem to know what was going on. He seemed to be unaware of what was happening. Now, I don't think -- we're not claiming he was totally unaware of what was happening, but he certainly was not aware of the details of what was happening. As the Trial Chamber held, he was very, very occupied with the situation at Zepa. And again - and we're going to go into this more this afternoon and tomorrow - the only direct evidence of his involvement was that July 15th telephone conversation with Colonel Beara in which you can legitimately infer General Krstic's knowledge that men were being killed -- not, mind you, a genocidal plan, but that men were being killed. And it is our submission - and we'll be speaking to that in more detail later - that he never did anything to further the enterprise. He didn't participate in that sense. When Mr. Marcussen said he participated, certainly he never did anything to aid and assist in the executions. As I say, he did know about the killings, but he really never was part of the plan to kill the men. And I don't think he was indispensable in any way, even to that third operation. Now, the Drina Corps, to the extent that assets were being used from the Drina Corps, and there's no evidence that General Krstic himself ever -- ever authorised the use of specific assets of personnel. To the extent, though, those that they were used, certainly the Drina Corps would be indispensable, but not General Krstic. So that is our submission on the sentencing issue. There was a lot more -- a lot more we said in our brief. We'd like to leave that to Your Honours to peruse, which I'm sure you will. Mr. Marcussen didn't spend any time really on Rwanda, or very little time. I'm going to spend virtually no time on it, because I think it's not very useful at all to engage in analysis of the cases there. Every case is unique. The Rwanda situation is a documented genocide; 800.000 people killed, a number of the defendants who were sentenced there actually personally took part in the killings. It's a completely different situation than what we have here. I'd like to turn now to the cumulative-conviction issue. And I have to say after listening to my learned colleague of the Prosecution, and after listening to my questions from the Court, I say in all sincerity - and I know I speak for Mr. Petrusic too - that the Defence team are children on the fringes of knowledge in this area. We don't purport to have the depth of understanding or knowledge that the Prosecution has in this case or, indeed, the members of the Court. We understand that there's -- that the case is of limited practical importance, as far as General Krstic is concerned, and that with it all the Prosecution is not asking for any increase in sentence as a result of their argument on cumulative convictions. There was a single sentence imposed of 46 years, following a very careful consideration by the Trial Chamber. If the Appeals Chamber affirms the conviction or some part of it, we would very respectfully ask - and again, I don't know if this is within Tribunal practice - but we would respectfully ask you to add to any judgement that if you decide that additional convictions should have been entered, that you note that if -- that General Krstic or suggest -- again, this can be the inclination of the Appeals Chamber -- that as a result of any additional convictions being added, that General Krstic not be prejudiced by this, that he still serve the sentence he would have served under the Trial Court's holding. There was a single sentence, based on a short period of activity, and we think a single sentence certainly was appropriate. We certainly disagree with the amount -- the number of years imposed here. And again, we've -- we've set this forth in some detail in our brief. And I refer Your Honours to that. The only other matter I'd like to say on cumulative convictions is: Musema was in French for quite a long time. It's no barrier to my learned friend here, of course. But it's now in English, and we have read it, and we do think their point is well taken on that. I think that the -- certainly the Chamber could enter convictions for extermination and genocide. I say that, certainly, it appears to be that way from Musema. Again, we don't have the depth or the sense of nuance that the members of this Court have, or indeed that the Prosecution have, but certainly on reading Musema we think the Prosecution's point is probably well taken on that. On the remaining cumulative-conviction issues, we do think that the Trial Chamber tried to come up with a common sense practical resolution. We tried to support that in our trial brief, and we would like to leave the -- leave that to the Chamber. In other words, what we said in our trial brief we would submit now to the Chamber. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sepenuk. Would my colleagues want to ask questions now, or would they want to ask questions after lunch?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: After lunch. So I take it if there are no comments at this stage from the Prosecution, we can now adjourn. And let me just look at the timetable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay. We -- we gained, thanks to the briefness of the argument by Mr. Sepenuk, which we much appreciate, we have gained some time; and therefore, we will be able to adjourn as previously planned, until 2.45. The Court will now rise. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.51 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Now we shall have a reply by the Prosecution. Twenty minutes have been allotted to that, and I understand that you might not need the entire time, but in any event please go ahead, and we'll see how it goes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour -- Your Honours, I -- I will not address a number of the issues raised by -- by the respondent. I don't find that necessary. We have briefed most of the issues already. So I will concentrate on one particular issue, where -- one particular aspect of the respondent's submissions, where we find it necessary to provide a reply. In support of the respondent's arguments that the sentence should not be increased, the respondent relied on a number of factual arguments. This does not directly respond to the Prosecution's ground of appeal, but as the respondent has relied on these factual propositions, in order to argue that the sentence should not be increased, we find it necessary to just make some clarifications with respect to what the Trial Chamber's findings were on the issues raised by the respondent in support of this argument. I'm not implying anything intentional there in regard to what the respondent said, in terms of -- of his view of the record, but I would like to state our reading of the judgement on a number of issues. It's essentially four or five issues that the respondent addressed. The respondent first stated that as a matter of fact he essentially had no knowledge of the crimes being committed at Potocari, and maybe even more generally the crimes being committed after the fall of Srebrenica in general. Your Honours, the Prosecution submit that the Trial Chamber's factual findings show otherwise. The respondent planned the attack on Srebrenica. In so doing, he stated in his testimony at pages 2163 to 2165 that he had knowledge of and prepared the plan, among other things, in pursuant to directive number one, issued by Karadzic in March 1995. Your Honours, at paragraph 28 of the judgement, parts of directive number one are quoted. I will just quote one sentence: "The directive directs that by planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope for future survival and life of the inhabitants of Srebrenica." In preparing prepare the plan for the attack on Srebrenica, the respondent had knowledge of this directive and the plan was to implement this. He was in charge of the operation at Srebrenica, and the Trial Chamber finds at paragraph 335 that he was no ordinary participant. The Trial Chamber finds that he could see the shelling of Srebrenica on the 10th and the 11th and that that -- those two days of shelling essentially was calculated to terrorise the civilian population and to drive them out from Srebrenica; that's paragraph 125. The day after the shelling had stopped, on the 11th, the respondent was standing next to General Mladic in the centre of Srebrenica town when General Mladic said that the moment has finally come to take revenge on the Turks here." In the Prosecution's respectful submission, this clearly show that the respondent -- well, these factual findings by the Trial Chamber show that the respondent did indeed have knowledge of the plan. At paragraph 337, and I quote, "The Trial Chamber finds that General Krstic was well aware that the shelling of Srebrenica would drive out tens of thousands of Bosnian Muslim civilians from the town and into a small area -- the small area of Potocari." He must have known, inevitably, the basic needs for food and water and medicine at the site would be -- would prove overwhelming. The Trial Chamber finds -- further finds, excuse me - that General Krstic was fully appraised of the VRS territorial goals in the Srebrenica enclave, which included cleansing the area of the Bosnian Muslim population. So this is the factual backdrop for the crimes that follows. And the Trial Chamber finds that he, the respondent, was fully aware of this situation. So the Prosecution submit that based on this evidence alone there's no basis for the factual proposition by the appellant put forward in his response to our appeal, that he essentially did not know what was going on. Now, there are other findings that are not going to -- with respect to the genocidal campaign. I discussed those at length earlier on, and it's outlined in our brief, so I will not touch on that. The respondent further put forward the factual proposition in support of his argument that the sentence should not be increased, that essentially anyone could have organised the buses, and that he was sort of insignificant in that respect. Your Honours, again, the Trial Chamber's findings are as a matter of fact otherwise. At paragraph 608, the Trial Chamber finds that the respondent played a significant role. It is not consistent with the interpretation of the facts that he was just an insignificant bystander or somebody who happened to have been asked to help out. The respondent also referred to Karadzic's order to take Srebrenica from the 9th of March -- 9th of July, in the evening, and referred to the fact that in that order it is directed that the Geneva Conventions have to be complied with. Your Honours, the factual findings by the Trial Chamber about how that attack took place, and especially what was done to the civilians during that attack, simply show that this part of the order either was not carried out or was actually never meant to be taken seriously. And interestingly, in this context, my learned colleague himself referred to the evidence from Deronjic that the Hotel Fontana meeting and the offers to the Muslims that they could stay was a mere smokescreen. With respect, Your Honours, the same would seem to have been the case with the reference to the Geneva Conventions, or at least, even if Karadzic had meant it, that part of the order was certainly not implemented during the attack on Srebrenica, for which the respondent was a crucial participant and had responsible -- was responsible for the coordination of the attack. My kind colleague draws my attention to the fact that I might have said that I quoted from a directive number one. What I quoted from was directive number seven. In any event, what I attempted to quote from was from paragraph 28 of the judgement, so I hope that that would create no confusion. The respondent was also put forward as a factual proposition that he had, well, almost as a humanitarian act ensured that the refugees from Potocari were put to buses and quickly sent away from the terrible humanitarian conditions that they were in when they were in the UN compound and around the UN compound. Your Honours, it's an interesting interpretation, but I'd like to stress that this was actually considered a criminal act. This was actually the act which was the implementation. This was how the forcible transfer was carried out. So we do not agree with this interpretation. The respondent also referred to an instruction that nobody could be harmed during the transfer of the civilians out of the Serb-held areas. The Prosecution is not purporting that there's any finding that this is a smokescreen, but as a matter of fact the Trial Chamber found that soldiers were hitting civilians as they were boarding the buses - in paragraph 48 of the judgement - that the buses were overcrowded and unbearably hot; also, the DutchBat -- the UN forces were not allowed to escort the buses to make sure that the civilians arrived safely at their destination; and men who were trying to board the buses, in this purported humanitarian act, were not allowed to get on and were later taken to the "White House," where they were detained along with the other people -- the other men who had been separated out from the group. And at Cerska the buses were stopped specifically for the purpose of separating -- of taking out any men that might have been overlooked before they left Potocari. Those men were also taken to detention facilities and subsequently executed. The findings on this point I refer Your Honours to paragraph 53 to 59, and 368 to 369 in the judgement. The Prosecution also notes that the buses subsequently were -- that were used for the transfer of the civilians, or at least some of the buses, subsequently were diverted to transport Bosnian Muslim men to massacre sites at Kravica, findings at 217 and 215, and that buses were diverted to transport the prisoners that were -- that were captured on the road. I think maybe I'm wrong on the Friday; I think it was a subsequent day. Those findings are found at 156 to 161 in the judgement. Finally, the respondent put forward as a factual proposition that, as I understand it - and maybe I misunderstood him - but I did understand my learned colleague as saying that there was essentially only one act of participation, which was the sending of Bratunac soldiers to participate in the Branjevo Farm execution. With all due respect, again, the Trial Chamber's findings were something else. So the respondent is putting this forward as a factual proposition as to what the judgement found and why our sentencing appeal should be dismissed, then we submit that he -- well, that the judgement shows otherwise. Let me just put it that way. And I apologise to my learned colleague. It's my lack of a proper command of English. It's not that I am purporting that there had been any attempt to misguide the Chamber. The Trial Chamber's findings were that there was substantial and compelling evidence to show that between the 14th and the 17th of July, resources of subordinate Drina Corps brigades were utilised in the mass executions and that the Drina Corps Command must have known of its subordinate unit's involvement in the executions; paragraph 296 of the judgement. The Trial Chamber also found specific acts of participation with respect to the six massacre sites that I mentioned this morning. With respect to Orahovac execution site, the Trial Chamber found that brigade guards -- brigade members were guarding the prisoners and their -- and that brigade vehicles were used for the transportation to the execution fields and assisted in the subsequent execution and participated in burials. With respect to Petkovic Dam, the Trial Chamber found that elements of the brigade transported prisoners to the detention sites -- from the detention sites - sorry - to the execution sites and participated in the burials; active participation; 231 to 232. With respect to Branjevo Farm, the Trial Chamber found that Drina Corps assets were an integral part of these executions. Popovic, the assistant commander for security, was heavily involved and monitored and reported on the operation. The Drina Corps Command organised fuel for the execution; they were essential to the transport and execution of the prisoners. Drina Corps Command played an organising role and coordinating role, and Drina Corps military police -- military police guarded prisoners in the buses that took them to the site where they were killed. Subsequently, Zvornik Brigade equipment were used to bury the victims. On the 16th of July, at Pilica Cultural Dom, Bratunac -- elements of the Bratunac Brigade were found to have participated in the killings. At Kozluk, Zvornik Brigade -- elements of the Zvornik Brigade participated in the burials of victims, and at Nezuk executions were carried out by -- with the participation of units under the command of the -- of the Zvornik Brigade. All this are factual findings by the Trial Chamber that they -- the Trial Chamber considered acts of participation in these crimes. And the Trial Chamber found at paragraphs 378 to 423 that the respondent had knowledge and directly participated in these crimes. Apart from the specific involvement, the Trial Chamber also summed up the respondent's participation as being that of -- or that he had a key coordinating role in the implementation of the killing campaign. I have not mentioned, Your Honours, the disputed intercepts. I know they're going to be discussed tomorrow. But in the Prosecution's submission, the intercepts from the 15th and 16th and 17th of July also show acts of participation. But I think I've already spent a long time responding to my colleague's -- or replying to my colleague's response, and I do not wish to take up any more of Your Honours' time with this. The basic point that the Prosecution have been trying to make is simply that to the extent that the respondent has relied on certain factual propositions, they are not supported by the Trial Chamber's findings, and therefore his arguments do not support -- well, first of all, they're not a response to our sentencing appeal; and secondly, those propositions do not support even his suggestion that the sentence should not be increased. This, Your Honours, completes my submission in reply. Thank you.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marcussen. We will now turn to the Defence, which will now have -- I'm terribly sorry.

So it now falls to me to say to you that I have seen over the interval your Prosecution appeal brief at page -- page 72, paragraph 5.3, where you referred to the matter, and I have also to acknowledge that I've seen the Tadic decision of 26 January 2000, at paragraphs 28 to, I think -- yes, 28, thereabouts, where the matter was discussed. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel, and thank you so much, Judge Shahabuddeen. Any other questions? Judge Guney, Judge Pocar? No. So we will now turn to additional submissions by the Defence. And you have one hour today, if that's all right, and you will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And may it please the Judges of this Honourable Court. The precise question -- we're going to start with the judgement issue. The precise question is whether the Trial Chamber erred in finding that there was a joint criminal enterprise which intended to destroy the Bosnian Muslim group in part at Srebrenica and whether General Krstic shared that genocidal intent. And I'd first like very briefly to set forth the legal principles that I believe this Tribunal has laid down over the last several years, the principles that I think will govern the appeal in this case. First of all -- and by the way, I'm doing this by way of just setting the context. I know that these principles are very well known to the members of the Court, but I want to set some context for our factual argument. Obviously genocide is a unique crime with special emphasis placed on specific intent or dolus specialis. As the Stakic Trial Chamber said recently, it's a crime that's distinguished by a surplus of intent. The intent must be to destroy the group in part. And as the Samardzija case pointed out, there is no numeric threshold of victims necessary to establish genocide. And as the Stakic Trial Chamber put it, "This Trial Chamber emphasises that in view of the requirement of a surplus of intent, it is not necessary to establish with the assistance of a demographer the size of a victimised population in numerical terms. It is the genocidal dolus specialis that constitutes the crime." A few more quotes on the question of numbers. I'm sure it goes without saying that General Krstic's lawyers are as appalled by the brutality and the horror of what happened at Srebrenica, as any civilised person should be. And we agree with one essayist on the subject who wrote - and I quote, "From a humanist point, it is quite repugnant to weigh the number of deaths which would accord significance in terms of the convention. Death and suffering are hardly matters for mathematical calculation." We subscribe to that completely. In a humanitarian sense, then, we speak of numbers reluctantly, but we must do so because historically and logically it's one method and one method only in determining genocidal intent. Numbers, of course, are also important in considering whether the perpetrator's intent was to destroy the group in substantial part, because the case law in both the ICTR and the ICTY have held that the crime of genocide by its very nature requires an intention to destroy at least a substantial portion of the group. And once the overall genocidal plan of action was established - for example, in the ICTR cases, as it was conclusively - the issue became only one of whether the killings by the individual defendants were pursuant to the genocidal plan. We don't have that in the ICTY cases. We do not have an unequivocal, documented intent as in Rwanda to destroy the group or part of the group. If a small number of persons are destroyed, it may not provide a sufficient basis for inferring genocidal intent. In Jelisic, less than a few hundred 100 individuals were killed, but there was a documented intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims of Brcko, since Jelisic openly styled himself as the Serbian Adolf and openly proclaimed his hatred of the Bosnian Muslim people and his desire to kill them. In Sikirica and Stakic, the numbers destroyed were higher. 1000 to 1400 people in Sikirica and some 3.000 in Stakic, many of whom in each case were killed at the Keraterm and Omarska detention camps. But these Trial Chambers held, first in Sikirica, that the numbers alone were an insufficient to show genocidal intent, and then in both cases that was not -- that there was not genocidal intent in any event, since the dominant purpose of the conduct was ethnic cleansing. In summary, on these general principles, the crucial factor in a genocide case is not just numbers killed but rather the determination of genocidal intent. A few hundred killings where the necessary intent is shown --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the benefit of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise for that. A few hundred killings where the necessary intent is shown may be sufficient to warrant a finding of genocide, as in the Jelisic case, as the Jelisic Appeals Chamber noted. But the killing of a multitude of people, as for example, the blowing up of a number of buildings containing thousands of people, or indeed the dropping of an atomic bomb, may not be genocide if not accompanied by the necessary genocidal intent to destroy and establish part of a group, as such. Continuing with general principles: How have Courts gone about the process of determining genocidal intent? The Trial Chamber in Stakic provided one answer to that question, as follows - and I quote - "It is generally accepted in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and the Rwanda Tribunal that genocidal dolus specialis can be inferred either from the facts, the concrete circumstances, or by a pattern of purposeful conduct." With these general principles as guides, I could like now to turn to our argument that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that there was a specific genocidal intent on the part of a joint criminal enterprise and on the part of General Krstic to destroy part of the Bosnian Muslim group as such. In determining whether genocide was committed as Srebrenica, the Trial Chamber considered two separate and uncontroverted sets of facts: First, that during the period 11 to 12 July 1995, approximately 25.000 Bosnian Muslims - most of them women, children, and elderly, who were living in the Srebrenica area - were transferred by Bosnian Serb forces to Bosnian Muslim-held territory; second, during the period 13 to 19 July 1995, as 10 to 15 thousand Bosnian Muslim men attempted to flee the area, many were taken prisoner and some 7500 Bosnian Muslim men were then executed. In holding that there was a joint criminal enterprise to commit genocide, the Trial Chamber stated as follows - this is at paragraph 594 - "The Trial Chamber concludes from the evidence that the VRS forces sought to eliminate all of the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica as a community. Within a period of no more than seven days, as many as 7 to 8 thousand men of military age were systematically massacred while the remainder of the Bosnian Muslim population present at Srebrenica, some 25.000 people, were forcibly transferred to Kladanj. The Bosnian Serb forces knew by the time they decided to kill all the military-age men that the combination of those killings, with the forcible transfer of the women, children, and elderly, would inevitably result in the physical disappearance of the Bosnian Muslim population at Srebrenica." After finding a joint criminal enterprise to commit genocide, the Trial Chamber concluded, with respect to the individual guilt of General Krstic, as follows - paragraph 634 - "Having already played a key role in the forcible transfer of the Muslim women, children, and elderly out of Serbian-held territory, General Krstic undeniably was aware of the fatal impact that the killing of the men would have on the ability of the Bosnian Muslim community of Srebrenica to survive as such. General Krstic thus participated in the genocidal acts of killing members of the group under Article 42(a) with the intent to destroy a part of the group."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm going to make a very measured effort now. In fact, I may go too slow now. I'm really going to try and do this right. Our submission is that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that genocide occurred at all under the facts presented at trial. The Trial Chamber correctly identified the protected group as the Bosnian Muslims. And in paragraph 560 -- 559 of the opinion. This is a detour here - the Trial Chamber specifically noted that the group was the Bosnian Muslims, not the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica, for other reasons, saying - and I quote - "The only distinctive criterion, that is, of the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica, would be their geographical location; not a criterion contemplated by the Convention." The Trial Chamber further correctly found that when considering an attempt to destroy a part of a group, the part must be a substantial part of the whole. However, when the Chamber compared the Bosnian Muslim men that were killed, it did not compare that part to the whole of the Bosnian Muslim group, some 1.4 million people, but, rather, looked to the effect that the death of the military-aged men would have on the ability of the Bosnian Muslim community to exist at Srebrenica. This comparison, we suggest, was erroneous in two ways: First, it diluted the numerical requirement of substantially; and second, it equated ethnic cleansing with genocide, an issue that I'll shortly address. Our submission is that the Trial Chamber erred in finding genocide, based on an intent to destroy a part - that is, the military-age men - of a part - that is, the Muslims of Srebrenica - of a protected group, and that being the Bosnian Muslims. The Trial Chamber, in our submission, should have compared the number of men killed, approximately 7500, to the whole of the Bosnian Muslim group, of 1.4 million people. Under that percentage, under that standard, the percentage is approximately one-half of 1 per cent of the Bosnian Muslim population; clearly an insignificant percentage standing alone to infer an attempt to commit genocide. The Trial Chamber never made that comparison; rather, the Trial Chamber concluded that the killing of the men had a substantial impact on the survival of the Bosnian Muslim population at Srebrenica. It is our submission that it was error for the Trial Chamber to conclude that the mass killings in Srebrenica were committed be the intent to destroy the group that resided there. The offence at Srebrenica must further be shown to have been committed within the context of an intent to destroy the group as such. This was the approach taken by the Trial Chamber in the Sikirica case, where it said: "There are two elements" - and I'm quoting now - "in the chapeau of Article 4(2), which the Prosecution is required as a matter of law to establish: First, it must establish the intent to destroy in whole or in part the Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian Croat population in Prijedor; secondly, it must also establish an intention to destroy the Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian Croat group as such. These two elements are cumulative; that is to say, the Prosecution must not only establish an intention to destroy the Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian Croat populations in whole or in part, but it must also establish this intention to destroy these groups as such." And then the Court in Sikirica went on to say, "Therefore, even if the evidence established an intention to destroy a part of the Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian Croat population, the Sikirica motion would still succeed because what was targeted was not the group as such but individual members of the group," and the Court went on to hold that acts of persecution were indeed proved but not genocide. The Krstic Trial Chamber never considered the second cumulative aspect that the Court spoke about in Sikirica. Had it done so, it would have had to conclude that there was no evidence that the killings in Srebrenica were done with the intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslim group as such. The Trial Chamber's conclusion that "by killing all the military-age men the Bosnian Serb forces effectively destroyed the community of the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica as such and eliminated all likelihood that it could ever re-establish itself on that territory" belies any intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslim people as such, as opposed to only displacing the Bosnian Muslim people from that territory. When I say "only," terrible as that may be, we're trying to make that distinction, only by displacing them, not destroying them. As William Schabas considered perhaps, the lead commentator on the law of genocide, stated in his recent Fordham Law Journal article, which, as Your Honours know, is attached to our Defence appeal brief and has now been officially printed, "would someone fully bent on the physical destruction of a group and cold-blooded enough to murder more than 7.000 defenceless men and boys go to the trouble of organising transport so that women, children, and the elderly could be evacuated?" Indeed, one may legitimately conjecture that the boys and the women were the significant part of the Bosnian Muslim group, since, as Mr. Schabas suggests, they in effect hold the key to the group's survival. In that sense, the deportation of the women and children from Srebrenica bears, we suggest, bears more, we suggest, on an intention to avoid committing genocide rather than an intention to commit genocide. Schabas -- Mr. Schabas also takes issue with the Trial Chamber's conclusion that the intent in killing the men and boys of military age was to eliminate the community as a whole. Schabas questions, at page 46 of his article, "can there not be other plausible explanations for the destruction of 7.000 men and boys at Srebrenica? Could they not have been targeted precisely because they were of military age and thus actual or potential combatants? Schabas concludes as follows: "As crimes against humanity, the atrocities in July 1995 in Srebrenica surely qualify, but characterising them as genocide seems to distort the definition unreasonably." I'd like to turn to our second argument on why we think the Chamber erred in the genocide finding, and that is that the Chamber erroneously equated displacement of a population of ethnic cleansing with genocide. As the Trial Chamber put it - and nowhere is this more evident than in paragraph 594 of the opinion - "The Trial Chamber concludes from the evidence that the VRS forces sought to eliminate all of the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica as a community." The Court goes on to say, "The Bosnian Serb forces could not have failed to know that by the time killed all the men that this selective destruction of the group would have an lasting impact upon the group. Their death precluded any effective attempt by the Bosnian Muslims to recapture their territory." Finally, the Court said, "The Bosnian Serb forces knew by the time they decided to kill all of the military-age men that the combination of these killings with the forcible transfer of the women, children, and elderly would inevitably result in the physical disappearance of the Bosnian Muslim population at Srebrenica." Moreover, in its judgement, the Trial Chamber states as follows: "The Prosecution points us to the terrible impact the events of 11-16 July had upon the Bosnian Muslim community in Srebrenica. What remains of the Srebrenica community" -- this is quoting from what the Prosecution said -- "survives in many cases only in a biological sense, nothing more." We respectfully suggest that if the Srebrenica community does survive in a biological sense, which it does, then no genocide was committed at Srebrenica. Again, in his law journal article on this precise holding of the Trial Chamber, Mr. Schabas had this to say - and I quote - "There is a world of difference between physical destruction of a group and a lasting impact upon a community. If the intent of the Serb forces was to have a lasting impact on Srebrenica's Muslims and they did not intend to destroy the community, the classic genocides of the twentieth century, those of European Jews and Rwandan Tutsis are distinguished by the insistence upon killing the women and children, precisely to ensure that the group is effectively destroyed." If the community survives in a biological sense, as it does here in the presence -- in the persons of the women, children, and surviving men, then it is our submission that genocide was not committed. This is consistent with the purpose of the genocide statute, as well as the wording of the Statute itself, to which I will very shortly turn. Mr. Schabas in his treatise entitled "Genocide in international law" states at page 196, "There is no doubt the drafters of the Convention quite deliberately resisted attempts to encompass the phenomenon of ethnic cleansing within the punishable acts." In this regard, we think it is also significant to note the in the Eichmann trial which took place in the District Court of Jerusalem, the Court stated, "The implementation of the final solution in the sense of total extermination is to a certain extent connected with the cessation of emigration of Jews from the territories under German influence." Until mid-1941 when the final solution emerged, the Israeli Court said, "A doubt remains in our minds whether that was here that specific intention to exterminate, as required by the definition of 'genocide.'" the Court stated that it would deal with such inhuman acts as being crimes against humanity rather than genocide. The Court therefore acquitted Eichmann of genocide for acts prior to August 1941 that dealt primarily with emigration rather than killings. And of course, all this is aside from the findings in the Sikirica and Stakic cases that expulsion of a group does not amount to genocide. So to summarise, our second ground for reversal of the Trial Chamber's findings is that it improperly concluded that the murder of the Bosnian Muslim men, together with the transfer of the women and children, amounted to genocide. The forced transfer of the civilian population was just that, a transfer for which General Krstic was convicted. The murder of the Bosnian Muslim men may have constituted acts of murder, persecution, and extermination, for which General Krstic was also convicted - and Mr. Petrusic will talk a bit about that tomorrow - but these crimes, extermination, murder, persecution, stand alone. Taken together they are not genocide. Finally, the trial judgement itself strongly indicate that the plan of the Bosnian Serb army was to ethnically cleanse the area and not to commit genocide. The Trial Chamber found that the plan for Krivaja '95 was a step toward the Serb goal of plunging the Bosnian Muslim population into humanitarian crisis and ultimately eliminating the enclave. That's paragraph 121 of the judgement. The continued shelling of the Serbian forces, after the original objectives of Krivaja '95 had been accomplished was to "terrify the Bosnian Muslim population and drive them out of Srebrenica"; judgement paragraph 125. There's no doubt that the terrorisation intensified and mass killings subsequently occurred, but the Trial Chamber itself found at paragraph 360 that acts of murder were not even contemplated at Srebrenica until as late as 11/12 July 1995, when the VRS became aware of the presence of men at Potocari and the escaping column of Bosnian Muslim men.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Counsel please slow down, especially when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm going to truly make an effort to be very, very measured. Our submission is that a reasonable Trial Chamber, applying the presumption of innocence, should have concluded that the intent of the perpetrators was what it had been from the start, to ethnically cleanse the area of the Bosnian Muslims, not to eliminate the group as such in a physical or biological sense. The Trial Chamber here reached an inferential conclusion of genocidal intent, despite the more logical conclusion that the executions of the military-age men were because they were of military age and that the forced transfer of the women, children, and elderly from Srebrenica was to ethnically cleanse the area and not to physically or biologically destroy the group. In making this finding of an intent to commit genocide by a joint criminal enterprise, as well as their finding relating to the individual intent of General Krstic, we believe that the Trial Chamber has not followed the law of this Trial Chamber as set forth in the Delalic appeal judgement, which I mentioned the other day. And that, of course, requires particularly in a circumstantial evidence case, as here, that factual conclusions "must be established beyond reasonable doubt. It is not sufficient that it is a reasonable conclusion available from that evidence. It must be the only" - underline, only - underlined in the opinion - "reasonable conclusion available. If there is another conclusion which is also reasonably open from that evidence which is consistent with the innocence of the accused, he must be acquitted." The Trial Chamber in the Vasiljevic case put the matter another way, based on the same legal principle - where the Prosecution -- and I quote here - "Where the Prosecution relies on proof of state of mind by inference that, inference must be the only reasonable inference available on the evidence." The Trial Chamber in the Krstic case, while acknowledging that his was a case which was based upon "layer upon layer of circumstantial evidence" nevertheless resolved a number of the key factual issues in the ase by making presumptions which we suggest were not the only reasonable conclusions from the evidence. We've set forth a number of these holdings of the Trial Chamber, mostly -- in our brief. That's, I believe, it's page 31 to 33. And mostly conclusions by the Trial Chamber, that General Krstic "must have known" or "could not have failed to know", or "could only surmise that"; that kind of thing. We mention these principles of law now, since they become even more relevant when we discuss later the Trial Chamber's holding that General Krstic intended to commit genocide. I'd like to take a very brief detour here now and talk about Mr. Deronjic's testimony. As Your Honours know, it's our position that the decision to kill the men was indeed a last-minute decision, that materialised, as the Trial Chamber held, on the evening of July 11th or the morning of July 12th. The only thing that derogates from that conclusion was the appearance in the testimony of Mr. Deronjic the other day. And I've taken notes on his testimony, and we think there's nothing in his testimony which would -- should cause Your Honours not to accept the judgement of the Trial Chamber on this issue. And I'd like to proceed with my analysis of Deronjic's testimony. My notes show that his testimony was this: On July 8th and 9th, 1995, he had a conversation with Karadzic about the Western Slovenian principle. It was not a plan, it was discussed as a possibility. And two options were mentioned: One, reduce the enclave to its urban core, or take over the town of Srebrenica. Now, the Western Slavonian principle was mentioned; kill them all, kill all the people. And Western Slavonian, of course, was that -- described a situation involving indiscriminate shelling of civilians and military fleeing a town. Well, for one thing, we don't have that in our case. We don't have indiscriminate shelling of civilians and military fleeing a town. What we do have is - there's no question we do have shelling of Srebrenica, and I believe there's also shelling of the -- some of civilians on their way to Potocari - if that indeed was the carrying out of the Western Slavonia principle, it was over by July 9th, July 10th at the latest. And again on July 9th, Mr. Karadzic issues that is order. Remember Prosecution Exhibit 432. And General Tolimir signed the order, but it quotes President Karadzic as saying, "For goodness sakes, treat the civilians with care. Don't harm the civilians," that kind of thing. So if there was this notion of destroying everybody, it was gone. That was just a tentative thing. It was a conversation, a brief conversation between two people. We claim that nothing ever eventuated from that. And if the shelling of Srebrenica and the civilians on the 8th and 9th and 10th constitutes the Western Slavonian principle, it was over by then. And, of course, the civilians were subsequently bussed to safety. And everything that happened thereafter was consistent with a change of plan. For example, Mr. Deronjic attending the meeting at the -- at the Fontana Hotel at the direction of -- of Mr. Karadzic, talking to the civilians and talking about the option to stay, to go to a third country, that kind of thing. Now, Mr. Deronjic says that was a smokescreen. And it very well -- it may very well have been a smokescreen. Again, as we said before, not a smokescreen that General Krstic was privy to, but a smokescreen to cover up the forcible transfer of the civilians. But, of course, that has nothing to do with any kind of a smokescreen to cover up killings. The next -- the next conversation note was on July 13th, when prisoners are being held in Bratunac, and Mr. Deronjic asks President Karadzic what to do, and the short of it is -- remember there was that coded message, and then -- which Deronjic interpreted to mean we're going to take the -- the people in custody in Bratunac and send them to the area Bijeljina at the Batkovici camp. And Deronjic is told by Karadzic that someone will come to tell him how to deal with the prisoners in Bratunac. And again, he interprets the coded comments to mean go to Batkovic. Well, then Colonel Beara arrives. And as Deronjic testified, he doesn't know who sent Colonel Beara. He has no idea. But Beara says he has orders from the top to kill the prisoners in Bratunac. Deronjic tells Beara that he has specific instructions from President Karadzic that no prisoners are to be killed in Bratunac and they are to be moved. Beara, who's the head of security for the Main Staff, a close ally of General Mladic, worked for General Mladic -- no love lost between General Mladic and Mr. Karadzic -- Beara is under the direct control of General Mladic. He reluctantly complies with the order of the civilian Deronjic. Beara had to have come on instructions from somebody besides Karadzic. If Beara had come from Karadzic, Deronjic could not have bluffed him by saying that he had orders from President Karadzic. If Beara's orders were also from Karadzic, his response would not have been reluctant compliance but, rather, to tell Karadzic -- Deronjic that his orders were also from the president. He did not do this. The only way he could be put aside by Deronjic, the only way Beara could be bluffed by Deronjic, was that if he was acting on orders from Mladic, the top of the command, and believed that those orders were overridden by direct order of the president, who was the Supreme Commander. And that it was Mladic who ordered the killings is further confirmed by the testimony of Mr. Obrenovic. And I refer now to the argument that Mr. Daniel Moylan, the Prosecutor, the Appeals Chamber, made the other day. I have a transcript of it. He summarised it of Mr. Obrenovic said when he was testifying recently. He said, "Mr. Obrenovic has said at the Nikolic trial" -- which has now been incorporated here - that's part of our additional evidence - "that on the 13th of July his security chief came to him as he was serving as acting commander of the Zvornik Brigade and advised him that he had -- that the security chief had been informed of a plan to execute the Muslim prisoners and that they would be transported to Zvornik to be executed." Mr. Obrenovic at that point responded, "We can't undertake such an operation without support of our -- first of all, our brigade commander, but also without reporting to the Drina Corps, which would be General Krstic, and the Drina Corps command." And the response from the security chief is quite telling because he said - and this is the Prosecutor speaking - because he said - quoting - "there's no need to report", quoting Obrenovic. "The orders came from Mladic, and our commander knows" - meaning the brigade commander - and everybody knows." So again, there's no reason, we respectfully suggest, that the Appeals Chamber should not pay respect to the finding of the Trial Chamber that this was a last-minute decision to kill the Bosnian Muslim men reached on the evening of July 11th, the morning of July 12th to cope with what was turning into a disastrous military situation for the Serbs, and that is the escape and the movement toward Tuzla by the column of Bosnian Muslim men. I would like now to turn to a discussion of how the Trial Chamber arrived at its finding that the deportation of the women, children, and elderly was essential to its consideration of the issue of genocidal intent. I particularly say this in light of the fact that the Trial Chamber specifically recognised - this is paragraph 580 - the Trial Chamber specifically stated that "Customary international law limits the definition of genocide to those acts seeking the physical or biological destruction of all or part of the group." Our submission is that the Trial Chamber enunciated this legal principle requiring physical or biological destruction, but then clearly deviated from it, based largely on language contained in the 1994 final report of the commission of experts. And I want to pause here for a moment. The greatest single failing of our briefs in this case was not even mentioning the commission of experts. Our brief -- just to give some historical background here, Your Honours -- was submitted under rather severe time constraints. There is some brief mention of the commission of experts in the Prosecutor's brief, but I think the single greatest disservice that we've done to this Chamber so far is not to discuss with any adequacy whatsoever the pivotal and fundamental role played by the report of the commission of experts in the Trial Chamber's opinion. And one of the main reasons for our submission of the additional appendix, the one that Your Honours admitted into evidence on November 7th, a recent admission, Annex 3 to our Defence appeal brief. It contain a number of documents which relate -- which give not only addition until history of the genocide convention and its commentaries. There's quite a substantial amount in there on the report of the commission of experts. Because our submission is that the Trial Chamber enunciated the legal principle about physical destruction but then took into account the forcible transfer of the civilians, equated that, then, the combination of two, with genocide because of specific language it relied on in the 1994 final report of the commission of experts. And I'd like to spend a fair amount of time on that, because it was so crucial to the Trial Chamber's opinion. The 1994 report of the commission of experts of the former Yugoslavia concluded that the intention to destroy the fabric of a society through the extermination of its leadership, when accompanied by other acts of elimination of a segment of society, such as deportation, could be deemed genocide. This is the so-called qualitative test to determine genocide. The idea of -- this idea of the commission of experts was discussed in the Jelisic and Sikirica cases, where ultimately the Court did not find that the actions in those cases met the qualitative test for genocide. The Trial Chamber in Krstic is the first Trial Chamber to make such a holding. In paragraph 634 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber stated as followings: "Finally, the Trial Chamber has concluded that in terms of the requirement of Article 4(2) of the Statute that an intent to destroy only part of the group must nevertheless concern a substantial part thereof, either numerically or qualitatively" - and that's what I stress, either numerically or qualitatively - "the military aged Bosnian Muslim men of Srebrenica do in fact constitute a substantial part of the Bosnian Muslim group, because the killing of these men inevitably and fundamentally would result in the annihilation of the entire Bosnian Muslim community at Srebrenica." In making that finding, the Trial Chamber totally adopted the argument contained in the Prosecution's final brief, relevant excerpts of which we've set forth in Part J to our Annex 3. And in its brief, the Prosecution relying on the report of the commission of experts argued as follows: "By killing the leaders and defenders of the group and deporting the remainder of it, the VRS and General Krstic had assured that the Bosnian Muslim community in Srebrenica and its surrounds would not return to Srebrenica, nor would it reconstitute itself in that region or indeed anywhere else." This, of course, was the precise finding of the Trial Chamber. They adopted the Prosecution's argument in toto. Because what the Court said at paragraph 595 is: "The Bosnian Serb forces knew by the time they decided to kill all of the military-age men that the combination of those killings with the forcible transfer of the women, children, and elderly would inevitably result in the physical disappearance of the Bosnian Muslim population at Srebrenica." As we expect to show, we believe that this finding of the Trial Chamber, based almost exclusively on the report of the commission of experts, is contrary to both the letter and the commentaries to the 1948 genocide convention. Our submission is that this report of the commission of experts established two principles of law, which were followed by the Trial Chamber in this case and should be rejected by this Chamber: First, the expert's report advanced the principle adopted by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 587 of the judgement, that the term "in part" in the genocide statute relates not only to a reasonably significant number relative to the total of the group as a whole, but also to a significant section of the group, such as its leadership; the commission of experts in finding that genocide could be established by the destruction of a significant section of the group, such as its leadership, cited as authority a 1985 United Nations report on the question of the prevention and punishment of the crime against humanity of genocide. This is the so-called --
