utterances.text: Would you kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I apologise again. This is the so-called Whitaker report, which we have reproduced in Annex 3, Section G that we submitted recently. The Whitaker report speaking of "The extent of destruction of a group," states, "in part would seem to imply a reasonably significant number relative to the total of the group as a whole or else a significant section of the group such as its leadership." As we expect to show, no language in the genocide statute or any of the accompanying drafts or committee reports or debates were cited by Mr. Whitaker to support this statement. Other than this single sentence and the report of commission of experts based on it, there is little, if any, support for the notion that a qualitative part of the group by way of its leadership should be considered as relevant in determining genocidal intent. Nor is there anything in the genocide statute or accompanying drafting history to support the Trial Chamber's conclusion in paragraph 587 that "Extermination specifically directed against law enforcement and military personnel may affect a significant section of the group in that it renders the group at large defenceless against other abuses of a similar or other nature." This language of the Trial Chamber is again based verbatim on the report of the commission of experts. The second principle emerging from the report of the commission of experts is that, as the Trial Chamber puts it - and I quote - "The attack on the leadership - this is paragraph 587 of the judgement - the attack on the leadership must be viewed in the context of the fate of what happened to the rest of the group. If a group suffers extermination of its leadership and in the wake of that loss a large number of its members are killed or subjected to other heinous acts, for example, deportation, the cluster of violations ought to be considered in its entirety in order to interpret the provisions of the convention in a spirit consistent with its purpose." This language, again, in the judgement was taken verbatim from the 1994 report of the commission of experts. Significantly, the Trial Chamber italicised the language, "In the context of the fate of what happened to the rest of the group." That's italicised in the Krstic opinion by the Trial Chamber, obviously referring to deportation, thereby showing unmistakably that deportation is a factor that ought to be considered in whether genocide was committed, a finding we believe to be erroneous. I'd like to turn now to an examination of the genocide statute and its accompanying commentaries and drafting history to demonstrate that the 1948 genocide statute was intended to embrace within its definition only those acts which demonstrate an intent physically or biologically destroy a protected group or part thereof. Now, other Trial Chambers, notably the Stakic Trial Chamber, has provided a very important and useful analysis dealing with this issue. But what we have found in our research over the last several months, additional materials which I don't think has ever been brought to the attention of any trial or appellate chamber. We think it's very important to present now. And we're going to focus on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. We will focus on demonstrating that the convention specifically excluded mass displacement of the population from the definition of genocide and further rejected the notion that elimination of a group's leadership could be considered as evidence of genocidal intent. I should like to begin very basically, very basically indeed, citing from the 3 May 1993 report of the Secretary-General pursuant to paragraph 2 of Security Council Resolution 808 of 1993. In that report, the Secretary-General states as follows, and I quote, "In view of the -- it is in the view of the Secretary-General, the application of the principle nullum crimen sine lege that the International Tribunal should apply rules of international humanitarian law which are beyond any doubt part of customary law. The part of conventional international humanitarian law which has beyond doubt become part of international customary law is the convention on the prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide." Now, I hasten to say that these principles, which were invoked in the Jelisic and Stakic decisions, are very, very well known to every member of this Chamber. The reason I mentioned it -- the reason I thought it worth mentioning, despite the fact that Your Honours know this stuff cold, is that because of a comment made by the Prosecutor in its brief, right at the outset of its brief at page 3, where they say "At the outset, the Prosecution notes that it is not the genocide convention of 1948 under which the appellant has been prosecuted but the crime of genocide as established at the relevant time pursuant to the Statute of the Tribunal." That is undoubtedly true, but I believe that the statement of the Prosecution set out at the beginning of its brief foreshadowed what we regard as a less-than-faithful adherence to both the letter and the drafting history of the 1948 genocide convention. And to support our argument, I'd like to turn now to the relevant analysis of the revisions of the convention leading up to the adoption of the final text of the convention. Prior to the final text, there were two drafts: The secretariat draft, the first draft, was prepared by the so-called experts, people like Raphael Lempkin, who coined the term "genocide" and who reportedly was the most energetic and zealous of those advocating the adoption of the genocide convention. The secretariat draft was then considered by the ad hoc committee, which was composed of the official representatives from several countries, including the United States, Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, Lebanon, China, France, and Venezuela. The work of the ad-hoc committee, after full discussion and debate evolved into the final draft of the convention. For the Appeal Chamber's information, the three principal drafts of the convention are set forth in Part E to Annex 3 of our brief. Significantly, Article 1 of the draft convention as originally presented read as follows -this is B2, Annex B [sic], page 2 - "in this convention, the word "genocide" means a criminal act -- when I say Annex B, it's Annex 3, Section B2. In this convention, the record "genocide" means a criminal act directed against anyone of the aforesaid groups of human beings with the purpose of destroying it in whole or in part" -- and then this language -- "or of preventing its preservation or development." "Or of preventing its preservation or development." The draft convention went to on determine the acts which would constitute acts of genocide. Some of these acts consisted of what the convention labelled "destroying the specific characteristics of the group" by the "forced transfer of children to another group" or "forced and systematic exile of individuals representing the culture of the group," and then a number of others were delineating. In explaining its draft, the drafters offered the following comments: "The act must be deliberate" -- I'm quoting now. Again, this is part C, Annex 3, parts C, page 2: "The act must be deliberate. This means that its object must be the destruction of human beings." And it goes on to say certain acts which may result --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down. We are really having problems in following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: By this definition - and I'm quoting now - certain acts which may result in the total or partial destruction of a group of human beings are in principle excluded from the notion of genocide. A number of matters are listed, including mass displacement of population. So that's the first indication that forcible transfer, ethnic cleansing, or what the drafters referred to as mass displacement of population specifically was not included as an act of genocide. The point was again made shortly thereafter in the same document, part C, 3, in our Annex 3, "Mass displacement of populations from one region to another -- to another also does not constitute genocide." After discussing physical genocide and biological genocide, the drafters went on to discuss cultural genocide, which was also proposed as a means of committing genocide. Under cultural genocide, there was a prohibition relating to forced transfer of children to another group. The second means of committing cultural genocide was as follows - and again, this relates to the commission of experts report. This was the second means, and it says this - I'm quoting part C, pages 6 and 7 - "Forced and systematic exile of individuals representing the culture of a group" - that's the title. "Such individuals are chiefly scholars, writers, artists, teachers, and educators, ministers of religion, doctors of medicine, engineers, lawyers, administrators, et cetera." It's their et cetera, not mine. The cultural -- it goes on: "The cultural and moral life of a group is sustained by its cultured members. If these are removed, the group is no more than an amorphous and defenceless mass." The report went on to say, and I quote, "Professor Lempkin expressed for the following wording, 'systematic elimination of the individuals representing the culture of the group by acts of violence or infringement of personal liberty.'" This draft convention was then submitted to the ad hoc committee on genocide. And the ad hoc committee report -- Annex 3, part D, 4 -- The committee stated "That it resolved not to take as a basis any of the drafting before it; namely, the secretariat draft, the draft by the United States of America, and the French draft, but to take them into account in its work. Specifically stating they were going to take into account the secretary draft. Significantly, after considering the draft conventions submitted by the experts, the ad hoc committee, while affirming the methods of committing physical and biological genocide further limited the manner in which cultural genocide could be committed. The convention draft, as the Chamber will recall, made genocidal the forced and systematic exile of individuals representing the culture of the group. That specific provision, that provision so relied upon, and that notion so relied upon by the commission of experts that somehow the destruction of leadership, the destruction of a qualitative portion of a group can constitute genocide, that was specifically eliminated from the ad hoc committee draft.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have to intervene once again. We are so sorry, but we don't have the text that is being read. And two booths are working into French and into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It's my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could I ask the counsel how long he's planning to continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I would say at least another -- I would say close to -- maybe 20 minutes -- 20 to 30 -- 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I may be as long as a half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could I ask, please, the interpreters, whether they would have enough strength, stamina, et cetera, to continue until 4.20 now. I can't hear you, the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are very tired because of the speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, let's, given the speed and the exhaustion of the interpreters, I suggest that you continue until 4.15 and then you will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. And I again -- once again apologise. Believe it or not, Your Honour, I was actually -- I thought I was making an effort to be quite slow here. And I apologise to the interpreters. And I will truly almost bore everybody to death now by how slow I will go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Well, try us. So until 4.15, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. So just to summarise very briefly, the provision about the forced and systematic exile of individuals representing the culture of the group was eliminated by the ad hoc committee, and also eliminated from that draft was the language making genocidal acts done for the purpose of "preventing the preservation or development" of a group. Surely the mass displacement of the population, including the expulsion of leaders of the community, relate not to physical or biological destruction but, rather, to "preventing the preservation or development of a group," a criterion which was specifically rejected by the committee. The final text of the convention, which Article 4 as adopted verbatim, eliminated all references to cultural genocide but added to the definition of genocide the following language: "E, forcibly transferring children of the group to another group." And that is indeed in the genocide statute of the Tribunal. The Appeals Chamber will recall that in the initial draft of the convention prepared by Professor Lempkin and his colleagues the forced transfer of children to another group was delineated as a means of committing cultural genocide, though virtually every other provision set forth as a means of cultural genocide was eliminated, either by the ad hoc committee or in the final draft the forced transfer of children to another group was added as the fifth and final act by which a genocidal intent could be determined. This is the only definition contained in the Statute which concerns the displacement of human beings as an act of genocide. But, of course, the provision is very specific. It relates only to children and obviously is designed to cover those acts where children are permanently transferred from one group to another, resulting in the displaced child losing his or her identity and culture. Clearly, by specifically limiting the acts of transfer or expulsion by which a genocidal intent can be inferred, the convention further expressed its intent that no other form of displacement should be considered as an act of genocide. I should add that this interpretation is further confirmed by the judgement of 31 July 2003 in the Stakic case. The Stakic decision noted the fact that the convention rejected a proposal by Syria to include: "Imposing measures intended to oblige members of a group to abandon their homes in order to escape the threat of subsequent ill-treatment," as a subsequent act of genocide. We've included the debate on that point in Section F of Annex 3. The Trial Court in Stakic rejected the Prosecution's argument that genocide had been committed in that case. In so holding, the Trial Chamber, after noting that cultural genocide, as distinction from physical and biological genocide, was specifically excluded from the genocide convention, also called attention to the comments of the International Law Commission that the definition of genocide -- that in the definition of genocide "the word 'destruction' must be taken only in its material sense, its physical or biological sense." The Stakic Trial Chamber went on to hold that "It does not suffice to deport a group or part of a group. A clear distinction must be drawn between physical destruction and mere disillusion of a group. The expulsion of a group or part of a group does not in itself suffice for genocide." Unlike the Trial Chamber in Stakic, and also contrary to the holding of the Trial Chamber in Sikirica, the Trial Chamber in Krstic held that the transfer of 25.000 women, children, elderly men from Srebrenica should be considered as an element of genocidal intent when coupled with the killing of the 7500 Bosnian Muslim men. As I hope we've shown, there's nothing in the genocide statute itself or in its drafting history or in the case law of the Yugoslavia or Rwanda Tribunals which support that finding of the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber's holding, as we've noted, is based on this 1994 final report of the commission of experts. It is this heavy reliance of the Trial Chamber on this report which we submit is perhaps the major error committed by both the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, who essentially provided the information to the Trial Chamber. That's -- and we regard it as really the major error committed by the Trial Chamber in this case. And we -- we're asking the Appeals Chamber to overrule this finding. And I believe it's necessary to set forth for the Appeals Chamber -- I want to give some history now of the 1994 commission of experts, how it came to -- how it was created, why it was created, because I don't think that the findings of the report of the commission of experts can be appreciated without some brief history of the recitation -- brief recitation of the history of this entity. Because as we'll show, the commission was established to gather evidence of violations of international humanitarian law, not to propose legal principles relating to genocide or other violations of international humanitarian law. Now, that history is largely set forth in Part H to Annex 3 of our appeal brief in a letter of 27 May 1994 from the Secretary-General to the president of the Security Council. In very brief summary, by Resolution of 6 October 1992, the United Nations Security Council requested the Secretary-General to establish a commission of experts to examine and analyse information gathered with a view of providing the Secretary-General with its conclusions on evidence of grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions and other violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. A five-member commission was appointed, chaired first by Professor Fritz Kalshoven, and following Professor Kalshoven's resignation, by Professor Serif Bassiouni.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I think we have reached the time limit that -- which we contracted with the interpreters. It would be fair to honour our commitment to them. They have been working so hard today. So I must ask you, Mr. Sepenuk -- I know how difficult it is to interrupt an argument midstream, but you will have to bear with us and continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I again apologise to the -- to the interpreters. I will really make a very, very strong effort to slow down. I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Court will now rise, and we will resume at 9.30 tomorrow morning.
